chapter.poland.subtitle: From the Legends to 1918
chapter.poland.title: Poland
level.barbara_secret.fact: Sigismund Augustus secretly married Barbara in Vilnius in the summer of 1547. When he became king in 1548, Queen Bona and the Sejm demanded a divorce; the king replied that he would sooner give up the crown. On 7 December 1550 Barbara was crowned in Kraków, and on 8 May 1551 she died — rumour blamed Bona for poisoning her, though there is no proof. The king followed the coffin on foot all the way to Vilnius. According to legend, the magician Pan Twardowski later summoned Barbara's spirit for him in a magic mirror.
level.barbara_secret.goal: The king secretly marries a Lithuanian widow, weathers the fury of his mother and the Sejm — and crowns her
level.barbara_secret.hint: First the wedding — a secret one. Then the storm: his mother and the Sejm demand a divorce. If the king gives in, Barbara will never wear a crown.
level.barbara_secret.intro: 1547. Young Sigismund Augustus, heir to the throne, is in love with Barbara Radziwiłł — the widow of a Lithuanian magnate, a beauty who is the subject of gossip. His mother, Queen Bona, hates the Radziwiłłs. The nobility considers the match beneath him.
level.barbara_secret.source: Letters of Sigismund Augustus; Łukasz Górnicki, The Deeds in the Polish Crown
level.barbara_secret.title: The King's Secret Marriage
level.belweder_1830.fact: On the evening of 29 November 1830, Second Lieutenant Piotr Wysocki roused the cadets of the Officer Cadet School; the signal was to be a fire at a brewery in Solec. The conspirators burst into the Belweder, but Grand Duke Constantine hid and then left Warsaw. The townspeople seized the Arsenal. On 25 January 1831 the Sejm declared Nicholas I dethroned from the Polish throne; a war began that lasted until the autumn. After the defeat the Kingdom of Poland lost its constitution and its army, and thousands of participants went into exile.
level.belweder_1830.goal: At the signal of a fire, cadets storm the Belweder, the grand duke flees — and the Sejm dethrones the emperor from the Polish throne
level.belweder_1830.hint: Without a signal no one will move. The grand duke did not die that night — he hid and fled. And the dethronement was done not with a dagger, but with words.
level.belweder_1830.intro: 1830. The Kingdom of Poland has a constitution, an army and a Sejm, but its king is the Russian emperor Nicholas I, and in Warsaw everything is run by his brother, Grand Duke Constantine. A conspiracy is brewing in the Officer Cadet School.
level.belweder_1830.source: Act of Dethronement, 25 January 1831; P. Wysocki, Memoirs
level.belweder_1830.title: The November Night
level.bona_sums.fact: In February 1556 Bona left for Bari, taking with her, so it was said, a treasury on twenty-four wagons. She lent Philip II 430,000 ducats. In November 1557 she was poisoned by her trusted courtier Gian Lorenzo Pappacoda — bribed, as contemporaries believed, by the Spanish — who then produced a will in Philip's favour. For two hundred years Poland demanded the return of the "Neapolitan sums" and received nothing. Bona left behind Italian vegetables: Poles still call the soup bundle of carrot, parsley and celery "włoszczyzna" — "Italian stuff".
level.bona_sums.goal: The queen leaves for Italy with the treasury, lends money to the King of Spain — and is poisoned, and the debt is never repaid to Poland
level.bona_sums.hint: You can only lend money you have with you. A courtier bought by the queen herself would not poison her — but that is not how it happened.
level.bona_sums.intro: 1556. The dowager queen Bona Sforza, an Italian who wielded power at her husband's court for forty years, has fallen out with her son. She decides to return to her Duchy of Bari, taking a huge treasury with her. The King of Spain, Philip II, who rules Naples, needs money.
level.bona_sums.source: S. Cynarski, Bona Sforza; Łukasz Górnicki, The Deeds in the Polish Crown
level.bona_sums.title: The Neapolitan Sums
level.byczyna_1588.fact: Maximilian besieged Kraków but could not take it and withdrew to Silesia. On 24 January 1588 at Byczyna, Zamoyski defeated his army and took the archduke prisoner; he spent thirteen months in Krasnystaw and in 1589 renounced the Polish crown. Zamoyski was chancellor, hetman and founder of Zamość, the Renaissance "ideal city" now on the UNESCO list. He is credited with the words: "Such will be the Commonwealths as the upbringing of their youth."
level.byczyna_1588.goal: The nobility elects two kings at once — and Hetman Zamoyski settles the dispute on the battlefield, capturing an Austrian archduke
level.byczyna_1588.hint: You can only fight once the pretender has been elected. The prisoner abdicates in favour of whoever stayed in the country — if Vasa leaves for Sweden, the throne will stand empty.
level.byczyna_1588.intro: 1587. King Stephen Báthory is dead. At the election the nobility split: Chancellor and Hetman Jan Zamoyski backed the Swedish prince Sigismund Vasa, while his enemies the Zborowskis backed the Austrian archduke Maximilian of Habsburg. Both were proclaimed king.
level.byczyna_1588.source: Reinhold Heidenstein, Commentaries on the Muscovite War; Budziński, Diary
level.byczyna_1588.title: Byczyna
level.cedynia_972.fact: On 24 June 972 at Cedynia, on the right bank of the Oder, Hodo's army was defeated; Thietmar of Merseburg writes that the Polish blow was struck by Czcibor, Mieszko's brother, and that of all the margrave's noble warriors only Hodo himself and the chronicler's father, Count Siegfried, escaped. The feigned retreat is a historians' reconstruction: the chronicle speaks only of the margrave's defeat, not of how he was lured. Emperor Otto I summoned both to judgement in Quedlinburg, and Mieszko had to send his son there as a hostage — the future Bolesław the Brave. Cedynia is the first battle in Polish history that we know of.
level.cedynia_972.goal: The prince retreats, the margrave gives chase — and the prince's brother strikes him from the rear
level.cedynia_972.hint: The margrave is stronger and cannot be beaten head-on — not even with a mustered retinue. Let him stretch his own line in the pursuit. But the blow must come from someone who did not run.
level.cedynia_972.intro: June 972. Without the emperor's knowledge, Margrave Hodo marches against Mieszko — for plunder and land on the Oder. His heavy cavalry is stronger than the Polish retinue. The prince has his brother Czcibor and knowledge of the river crossings.
level.cedynia_972.title: Cedynia
level.chocim_1621.fact: From 2 September to 9 October 1621 the camp at Khotyn repelled every assault by an army several times larger. Chodkiewicz died in the camp on 24 September, and Stanisław Lubomirski took command. The Cossacks of Sahaidachny, who was wounded in battle, made up almost half of the defenders. The sultan agreed to peace. On his return, Osman II blamed the Janissaries for the failure and planned to disband them — and in 1622 they killed him; it was the first regicide in the history of the Ottoman Empire.
level.chocim_1621.goal: A fortified camp, reinforced by the Cossacks, withstands the assaults of the sultan's huge army for a month; the hetman dies, but the camp holds
level.chocim_1621.hint: You cannot take the field against such an army. The strength lies in the camp and in those who came to it. And the hetman hands over his mace only as he is dying.
level.chocim_1621.intro: 1621. The young sultan Osman II leads a huge army against the Commonwealth. On the Dniester, by the fortress of Khotyn, it is awaited by the fortified camp of Hetman Jan Karol Chodkiewicz — he is over sixty and ill. The Zaporozhian Cossacks of Hetman Petro Sahaidachny are coming to help.
level.chocim_1621.source: J. Sobieski (the king's father), Commentary on the Khotyn War; J. Ostroróg, Diary
level.chocim_1621.title: Khotyn
level.chocim_1673.fact: On the night before 11 November 1673 Sobieski kept his army at battle readiness, and the Turks, expecting an assault, spent the night in armour in the frost. At dawn the infantry broke through the rampart and the hussars burst into the camp; Hüseyin Pasha's army was almost wiped out, many perishing when the bridge over the Dniester collapsed. On the eve of the battle, 10 November, King Michał Korybut Wiśniowiecki had died — the army did not yet know. On 21 May 1674 Sobieski was elected king.
level.chocim_1673.goal: The hetman keeps the Turks out in the frost all night awaiting an attack, takes their camp at dawn — and becomes king
level.chocim_1673.hint: A fortified camp cannot be taken head-on. Let the enemy tire before the battle begins. The nobility rewards victory with a crown — but only the victor.
level.chocim_1673.intro: November 1673. At Khotyn on the Dniester stands the fortified camp of Hüseyin Pasha's Turkish army. It is besieged by the army of the Commonwealth under Grand Crown Hetman Jan Sobieski. Cold, freezing rain.
level.chocim_1673.source: J. Sobieski, letters to Marysieńka; W. Kochowski, Climacterics
level.chocim_1673.title: Khotyn 1673
level.chopin_heart_1849.fact: Chopin died on 17 October 1849 and was buried in Père Lachaise cemetery, but before his death he asked that his heart be taken back to his homeland. At the start of 1850 Ludwika secretly carried it across the border in a jar of cognac — hidden, legend has it, under her skirt. The heart is sealed in a pillar of the Holy Cross Church in Warsaw. In 2014 scientists secretly examined the jar and confirmed that Chopin died of complications of tuberculosis.
level.chopin_heart_1849.goal: Chopin dies in Paris, and his sister secretly smuggles his heart across the border in a jar of cognac
level.chopin_heart_1849.hint: Nothing can be carried openly through customs. First the will, then the hiding place.
level.chopin_heart_1849.intro: 1849, Paris. Frédéric Chopin, who left Poland in 1830, is dying of lung disease at thirty-nine. He was never able to return home. His sister Ludwika is by his side.
level.chopin_heart_1849.source: Chopin family letters; findings of the 2014 examination
level.chopin_heart_1849.title: Chopin's Heart
level.copernicus_olsztyn.fact: In the winter of 1520–1521 Copernicus led the defence of Olsztyn: he strengthened the walls, gathered a garrison and wrote to King Sigismund asking for reinforcements; the Order never took the castle. On the wall of the Olsztyn gallery you can still see the table he drew for observing the Sun. The book On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres, in which the Earth revolves around the Sun, was published in Nuremberg in 1543; according to tradition, Copernicus received the first copy on the day of his death, 24 May. He studied in Kraków in 1491–1495 — a Kraków student, a "żak".
level.copernicus_olsztyn.goal: The astronomer-canon defends a castle against the knights of the Order — and then moves the Earth from the centre of the world
level.copernicus_olsztyn.hint: First the walls, then the sky. He can leave the war behind, but then the castle will fall.
level.copernicus_olsztyn.intro: 1520, Poland is at war with the Teutonic Order. The Warmian canon Nicolaus Copernicus, a graduate of the Kraków Academy, serves as administrator of the chapter's estates and lives in Olsztyn Castle. The Order's troops are burning the countryside and approaching the walls.
level.copernicus_olsztyn.source: Letters of Copernicus to King Sigismund I (1521); G. Rheticus, First Account (Narratio prima)
level.copernicus_olsztyn.title: Copernicus Holds Olsztyn
level.drzymala_1904.fact: Refused a permit, Michał Drzymała bought a circus wagon and moved into it: by law a wagon was not a house as long as it was moved every twenty-four hours — and he moved it. For years the authorities fined him and took him to court, newspapers wrote about "Drzymała's wagon", and he became a symbol of stubborn resistance to Germanisation. In 1909 the wagon was finally confiscated; Drzymała dug himself a dugout. Today a memorial wagon stands in Podgradowice.
level.drzymala_1904.goal: A Pole is forbidden to build a house on his own land — and lives for five years in a circus wagon, moving it every day
level.drzymala_1904.hint: Without land there is nothing to argue about. Building a house without a permit means losing it. The law speaks of houses, not wagons.
level.drzymala_1904.intro: 1904, Prussia. A new law forbids building houses on newly purchased land without the authorities' permission — and Poles are not given permission. This is how the authorities keep Poles from buying land. The peasant Michał Drzymała has bought a plot in Podgradowice.
level.drzymala_1904.source: Prussian colonisation law of 1904; press reports 1904–1909
level.drzymala_1904.title: Drzymała's Wagon
level.first_partition_1772.fact: On 5 August 1772 in St Petersburg the three powers signed a convention: Poland lost about a third of its territory and a third of its population. In 1773 the Sejm, under the guard of foreign troops, was to ratify the partition; the envoy Tadeusz Rejtan lay down across the threshold of the chamber, crying "Kill me, but do not kill the Fatherland!" — they stepped over him. Frederick II said of Maria Theresa, who had long hesitated: "She wept, but she took." Jan Matejko painted "Rejtan" in 1866, and the painting hangs in the Royal Castle in Warsaw.
level.first_partition_1772.goal: Three neighbours agree to carve up the Commonwealth, and a lone envoy lies across the threshold of the Sejm — but the partition is ratified all the same
level.first_partition_1772.hint: Three are dividing — and all three must agree. One man's protest will not stop the partition, but it has gone down in history. Stop it by force? Against the Prussian army there is nothing to fight with.
level.first_partition_1772.intro: 1772. The Commonwealth has been weakened by the war of the confederates and by foreign armies. Russia, Prussia and Austria decide to take a piece of its lands each — and to force the Sejm to ratify it.
level.first_partition_1772.source: St Petersburg Convention of 1772; Diary of the Sejm of 1773
level.first_partition_1772.title: The First Partition
level.gniezno_1000.fact: On 23 April 997 Adalbert was killed by the Prussians; Bolesław ransomed his body for its weight in gold and buried it in Gniezno. In March 1000 Otto III came to the tomb as a pilgrim, barefoot. Gallus Anonymus writes that the emperor took the diadem from his own head and placed it on Bolesław's, called him "brother and partner of the empire" and gave him a copy of the Holy Lance of Saint Maurice, receiving in return an arm of the saint. At that time an archbishopric was founded in Gniezno with bishoprics in Kraków, Wrocław and Kołobrzeg — the Polish Church became independent. Bolesław was crowned king only in 1025, a few months before his death.
level.gniezno_1000.goal: A saint dies among the Prussians, the prince ransoms his body for its weight in gold — and the emperor comes to the tomb as a pilgrim
level.gniezno_1000.hint: The emperor is coming not to the prince but to the saint: without the relics there is nothing to invite him to. The relics are with the Prussians — and war with them won't bring them back, it will only spoil the bargain.
level.gniezno_1000.intro: 997. Adalbert, former Bishop of Prague and friend of the young emperor Otto III, asks Prince Bolesław to let him go and preach to the pagan Prussians. Bolesław gives him a boat and an escort. The emperor dreams of a new Christian empire — a Rome that the Slavs will join.
level.gniezno_1000.source: Gallus Anonymus, I, 6; Thietmar of Merseburg, IV, 45–46; Life of Saint Adalbert
level.gniezno_1000.title: The Congress of Gniezno
level.grunwald_1410.fact: The heralds of Grand Master Ulrich von Jungingen brought Jagiełło two naked swords — these swords later became a symbol of the victory. Vytautas's Lithuanian banners withdrew — whether this was flight or a feigned manoeuvre, historians still argue — and some of the Order's knights rushed after them. Jagiełło committed his reserves, the Order's army was surrounded, and the Grand Master fell along with most of the brethren of the Order. Zawisza the Black of Garbów distinguished himself in the battle — ever since, Poles say "to rely on someone as on Zawisza". Malbork could not be taken after the battle, but the power of the Order was broken.
level.grunwald_1410.goal: The Grand Master sends the king two swords in mockery, the Lithuanians withdraw, the knights give chase — and the king strikes the disordered army
level.grunwald_1410.hint: The Order is strong as long as it holds its formation — even the finest knight cannot beat it alone. Let it break its own line in the pursuit. And the king is waiting for a challenge.
level.grunwald_1410.intro: 15 July 1410, a scorching day. On the field between Grunwald and Tannenberg the army of the Teutonic Order meets the allied armies of Poland and Lithuania — one of the largest battles of medieval Europe. King Jagiełło stands in the forest, hears Mass and does not begin.
level.grunwald_1410.source: Jan Długosz, Annals, XI; Chronicle of the Conflict of Władysław, King of Poland, with the Teutonic Knights
level.grunwald_1410.title: Grunwald
level.henri_flight.fact: Charles IX died on 30 May 1574; the news reached Kraków on 14 June. On the night of 19 June, after a feast, Henry slipped out of Wawel and galloped for the border of the Empire. Chamberlain Jan Tęczyński caught up with him near Pszczyna; the king, it is said, gave him a ring and promised to return. He did not: in Paris he became Henry III, and in 1589 he was killed by the monk Jacques Clément. A year later Poland declared the throne vacant, and Stephen Báthory was elected king — together with that same Anna Jagiellon.
level.henri_flight.goal: A French prince, king of Poland for only half a year, learns of his brother's death and flees Wawel by night — he is caught only at the border
level.henri_flight.hint: He would not have fled without a reason — first the news from Paris. Married to the Jagiellonian, he would have found it much harder to flee; the wedding never took place.
level.henri_flight.intro: 1574. Henry of Valois has been crowned in Kraków, but he is bored: a foreign language, endless Sejms, a promised marriage to the no-longer-young Anna Jagiellon. In France his brother, King Charles IX, is ill.
level.henri_flight.source: Jan Dymitr Solikowski, Brief Notes; P. Desportes, letters
level.henri_flight.title: The Flight of Henry of Valois
level.jadwiga_axe.fact: Jadwiga was crowned on 16 October 1384. William came to Kraków, but the lords drove him out; according to Długosz, the queen wanted to hack through the gates of Wawel with an axe and was stopped by Vice-Chancellor Dymitr of Goraj. On 14 August 1385 at Krewo, Jagiełło undertook to be baptised, to baptise Lithuania and to join it to the Crown. On 15 February 1386 in Kraków he was baptised with the name Władysław, three days later he married Jadwiga, and on 4 March he was crowned. Thus began the union of Poland and Lithuania and the Jagiellonian dynasty; Lithuania became the last pagan country in Europe to adopt Christianity.
level.jadwiga_axe.goal: The young queen gives up her beloved betrothed and marries a pagan Lithuanian prince — and two countries are joined for four centuries
level.jadwiga_axe.hint: The queen's heart belongs to William, and a secret wedding seems so simple. But then there will be no union and no baptism of Lithuania. First she must say no — and only then summon the Lithuanian.
level.jadwiga_axe.intro: 1384. Poland is ruled by ten-year-old Jadwiga — crowned "king", not queen, because a woman on the throne is not provided for. Since childhood she has been betrothed to the Austrian prince William. The Polish lords are seeking another husband for her: the Grand Duke of Lithuania, Jogaila, a pagan whose country is vast and surrounded by enemies.
level.jadwiga_axe.source: Jan Długosz, Annals, X; Act of Krewo (1385)
level.jadwiga_axe.title: Jadwiga and Jagiełło
level.january_1863.fact: The January Uprising began on 22 January 1863. The National Government operated underground: press, taxes, post, its own courts and police — and almost no one knew who belonged to it. On 2 March 1864, by decree of Alexander II, the peasants of the Kingdom of Poland received their land as property on more favourable terms than in Russia — largely to turn them away from the uprising. Traugutt was arrested in April 1864 and executed on 5 August on the slopes of the Warsaw Citadel together with four members of the government. Thousands of participants were exiled to Siberia.
level.january_1863.goal: The insurgents create an underground state with taxes and a postal service — and the emperor responds by giving the peasants land
level.january_1863.hint: In open battle against the empire's army they cannot hold out. The state is built in secret: first the government, then everything else. The emperor answers with more than troops.
level.january_1863.intro: 1863. An uprising begins in the Kingdom of Poland — a guerrilla war in the forests, without an army or fortresses. To hold out, the insurgents need an invisible state. In the autumn it is headed by a former officer, Romuald Traugutt.
level.january_1863.source: Documents of the National Government, 1863–1864; decree of 2 March 1864
level.january_1863.title: The Secret State
level.jasna_gora_1655.fact: From 18 November to 27 December 1655 some three thousand Swedes besieged Jasna Góra, defended by about seventy monks and a couple of hundred soldiers and nobles under Prior Augustyn Kordecki; the monastery held out. News of the defence spread across the country and helped raise an uprising against the Swedes. On 1 April 1656 in Lwów, John Casimir proclaimed the Mother of God Queen of Poland and promised to ease the lot of the peasants — a promise that was never kept. Henryk Sienkiewicz made the siege the centrepiece of his novel The Deluge, adding the fictional Kmicic, who blew up a Swedish cannon.
level.jasna_gora_1655.goal: A monastery defended by monks and a handful of nobles beats off the Swedes — and the whole country rises against the invaders
level.jasna_gora_1655.hint: The general will offer an honourable surrender; the prior did not yield. The king cannot take vows from Silesia — first he must return. And he took the vow once the monastery had already held out.
level.jasna_gora_1655.intro: 1655, the Deluge. The Swedish army has occupied almost the entire Commonwealth, magnates are going over to the Swedish king, and John Casimir has fled to Silesia. The Swedish general Burchard Müller approaches the Pauline monastery on Jasna Góra in Częstochowa — a shrine holding an icon of the Mother of God.
level.jasna_gora_1655.source: A. Kordecki, The New Gigantomachy; Samuel Pufendorf
level.jasna_gora_1655.title: Jasna Góra
level.kinga_salt.fact: The Hungarian princess Kinga was to marry the Polish prince Bolesław. Her father asked what he should give her as a dowry, and she asked not for gold but for salt — the salt her new homeland lacked so badly. Before leaving, Kinga went down into a Hungarian salt mine and threw her betrothal ring into its depths. When she arrived in Poland, she ordered the miners to dig near the village of Wieliczka. For a long time they found nothing — then suddenly a pickaxe struck a white block. When the block was split open, Kinga's ring glinted inside. Ever since, Wieliczka has given Poland its salt, and Kinga became the patron saint of miners; deep underground, a whole chapel has been carved out of salt in her honour.
level.kinga_salt.goal: A princess asks for salt as her dowry, throws her ring into a Hungarian mine — and it is found in the first block of salt at Wieliczka
level.kinga_salt.hint: Everyone has gold — Poland needs something else. The ring is thrown where you want to take the salt from. And it will be found by those who dig.
level.kinga_salt.intro: 1246. The Hungarian princess Kinga, daughter of Béla IV, is travelling to Kraków as the wife of Prince Bolesław the Chaste. Her father asks what to give her as a dowry. Hungary is rich in salt, while in Lesser Poland salt is an expensive import.
level.kinga_salt.source: Life of Blessed Kinga (14th century); Jan Długosz, Annals
level.kinga_salt.title: Saint Kinga's Ring
level.kircholm_1605.fact: On 27 September 1605 Chodkiewicz lured the Swedes off the hills with a feigned retreat, and the hussars overthrew the stretched-out army in a single charge; the Swedes lost, by various estimates, between half and two-thirds of their army. Charles IX himself escaped only because the knight Henrik Wrede gave him his horse and was killed. Congratulations came from the pope, the emperor and even the Shah of Persia. Kircholm is a model of what the Polish hussars could do, and their wings — wooden frames with feathers — became a symbol of the era.
level.kircholm_1605.goal: The hetman lures the Swedes off the hills with a feigned retreat — and the winged hussars rout an army three times larger
level.kircholm_1605.hint: On the hills the Swedes are invulnerable — head-on, and even with reinforcements. Let them come down by themselves. The hussars strike only at a stretched-out line.
level.kircholm_1605.intro: 1605. King Charles IX of Sweden leads an army of almost eleven thousand men against Riga. The Lithuanian hetman Jan Karol Chodkiewicz can field fewer than four thousand against it. The Swedes stand on the hills near the town of Kircholm.
level.kircholm_1605.source: S. Starowolski; J. Chodkiewicz, report to the king (1605)
level.kircholm_1605.title: Kircholm
level.klushino_1610.fact: On 4 July 1610 at Klushino Żółkiewski defeated an army several times larger than his own; some of the foreign mercenaries went over to his side. Two weeks later in Moscow Tsar Vasily Shuisky was deposed and forcibly tonsured as a monk. The boyar government, the "Seven Boyars", concluded a treaty with the hetman on 17 August: Prince Władysław would become tsar — on condition that he accepted Orthodoxy. King Sigismund would not let his son go and demanded the throne for himself; the treaty collapsed, and in November 1612 the Polish garrison in the Kremlin surrendered to the militia of Minin and Pozharsky. Shuisky was taken to Poland, where he died.
level.klushino_1610.goal: The hetman routs the tsar's army, the tsar is deposed — and the boyars agree to invite a Polish prince to the throne
level.klushino_1610.hint: The treaty is signed by the victor — so first the battle. And King Sigismund wanted the throne for himself, which must not happen in our story.
level.klushino_1610.intro: 1610, the Time of Troubles. The Polish king Sigismund III is besieging Smolensk. Hetman Stanisław Żółkiewski with a small force marches out to meet an army led by Tsar Vasily Shuisky's brother together with Swedish mercenaries.
level.klushino_1610.source: S. Żółkiewski, The Beginning and Progress of the Muscovite War; The New Chronicler
level.klushino_1610.title: Klushino
level.kosciuszko_1794.fact: On 24 March 1794 Kościuszko took the oath in the Kraków Market Square and became Commander-in-Chief of the uprising. On 4 April at Racławice, units of scythemen — peasants with scythes set upright on their shafts — took General Tormasov's Russian battery at a run. Wojciech Bartosz, according to tradition, was the first to reach a cannon and snuffed out its fuse with his cap; he was made an officer and was killed two months later. As a mark of respect, Kościuszko wore a peasant sukmana coat. The Racławice Panorama — a huge circular painting from 1894 — is today in Wrocław.
level.kosciuszko_1794.goal: The general swears an oath to the nation in the Kraków Market Square, calls on peasants with scythes — and the scythemen take an enemy battery
level.kosciuszko_1794.hint: Regular troops cannot be beaten head-on. The peasants will follow the one who swore an oath to the nation. And the guns are taken by those who have scythes.
level.kosciuszko_1794.intro: 1794. After the Second Partition only a stump of the Commonwealth remains. General Tadeusz Kościuszko — a hero of the American War of Independence — returns to Kraków to raise an uprising. There is almost no regular army.
level.kosciuszko_1794.source: Kościuszko's reports of 1794; J. U. Niemcewicz, Memoirs
level.kosciuszko_1794.title: Racławice
level.krzywousty_will.fact: Under the testament of Bolesław III, known from Wincenty Kadłubek's account, the senior member of the dynasty received Kraków and the seniorate province, while the younger sons received their own lands: Bolesław the Curly got Masovia, Mieszko the Old Greater Poland, Henry Sandomierz; the youngest, Casimir, got nothing. The principle of seniority was meant to preserve unity, but as early as 1146 the eldest, Władysław, tried to take his brothers' provinces, was driven out and died abroad — hence his nickname "the Exile". So began the period of fragmentation: Poland broke up into dozens of duchies and was reunited only under Władysław the Elbow-high, crowned in 1320. The original text of the testament has not survived.
level.krzywousty_will.goal: The duke divides the country among his sons so that they will not fight — and Poland falls apart into provinces for two hundred years
level.krzywousty_will.hint: Kraków to the eldest, by right of seniority; provinces to the younger ones. Leaving everything to one seems safer, but the brothers would not have waited. And a testament is written while the duke is alive.
level.krzywousty_will.intro: 1138. Bolesław Wrymouth has been at war all his life — with Germans, Czechs, Pomeranians and his own brother Zbigniew, whom he had blinded and later repented. Now he has several sons by two wives, and he wants them not to cut each other's throats after he is gone.
level.krzywousty_will.source: Wincenty Kadłubek, Chronicle, III, 26; Greater Poland Chronicle
level.krzywousty_will.title: Wrymouth's Testament
level.lech_eagle.fact: Three brothers — Lech, Čech and Rus — had long led their clans in search of a new land, until the road split three ways. Čech led his people south, climbed Mount Říp and said: here shall be our home. Rus went east, towards the rising sun. And Lech journeyed north through forests and lakes, until one evening at sunset he saw a nest in a mighty oak and above it a white eagle, its wings spread against the crimson sky. Lech knew it was a sign: here he built his stronghold and named it Gniezno, from the word for "nest", and he made the white eagle on a red field his coat of arms. The brothers parted ways but remained brothers — and that, they say, is how the Poles, the Czechs and the Ruthenians came to be.
level.lech_eagle.goal: Three brothers go their separate ways, and the one who stays builds a stronghold where he saw a white eagle
level.lech_eagle.hint: First the crossroads: each brother has his own road. Čech goes south to his mountain, Rus towards the rising sun. Lech settles not where the land is richest, but where he is given a sign.
level.lech_eagle.intro: Long, long ago three brothers led their clans from the south in search of new land. There is one road, but the people keep growing, and living together is cramped. It is time for the brothers to part: each will find his own land, but only the one who is given a sign will know exactly where.
level.lech_eagle.source: Greater Poland Chronicle (late 13th – early 14th century); Cosmas of Prague, Chronicle of the Czechs (c. 1120)
level.lech_eagle.title: Lech, Čech and Rus
level.legnica_1241.fact: On 9 April 1241 at Legnica, according to Długosz, the Mongols broke the knightly formation with a feigned flight and a smoke screen and cut it down with arrows; Prince Henry the Pious was killed, and his head was carried on a spear beneath the walls of Legnica. And in Kraków, legend says, the trumpeter on the tower of St Mary's Church was the first to see the Tatars approaching and sounded the alarm. An arrow pierced his throat mid-note — but the townsfolk heard the signal and managed to shut the gates. Ever since, the Hejnał has sounded from the tower every hour and broken off on that very note — in memory of the trumpeter who saved the city.
level.legnica_1241.goal: The Mongols break the knights' formation with a feigned flight and kill the duke, while a trumpeter on a Kraków tower sounds the alarm until an arrow cuts off the tune
level.legnica_1241.hint: The knights cannot be beaten head-on — they are strong as long as they hold formation. Let the pursuit break the line. And the alarm is sounded while looking the enemy in the face.
level.legnica_1241.intro: 1241. Batu's Mongol army is marching on Hungary, and one of its detachments, under Baidar and Orda, passes through Poland: Sandomierz is burned, Kraków is burned. At Legnica the Mongols are awaited by the Silesian duke Henry the Pious — with Polish knights, German volunteers and brethren of the knightly orders.
level.legnica_1241.source: Jan Długosz, Annals, VII; Silesian Chronicle; E. Kelly, The Trumpeter of Krakow (1928)
level.legnica_1241.title: Legnica and the Hejnał
level.leszczynski_1734.fact: In September 1733 some thirteen thousand nobles voted for Leszczyński; under the protection of Russian troops a small group of electors chose Augustus III. Leszczyński took refuge in Gdańsk, which in 1734 was besieged by the Russian army of Field Marshal Münnich; on 27 June he fled the city disguised as a peasant. The War of the Polish Succession began. In 1736 Leszczyński abdicated and received Lorraine for life — Place Stanislas in Nancy, built in his time, is now on the UNESCO list. He died in 1766 when his dressing gown caught fire from the fireplace.
level.leszczynski_1734.goal: The nobility elects a king by a huge majority, but foreign troops put another on the throne — and the chosen king flees Gdańsk disguised as a peasant
level.leszczynski_1734.hint: You can only flee from a siege. Holding out to the end means being captured. While one is besieged, the other is already being put on the throne.
level.leszczynski_1734.intro: 1733. By a huge majority the nobility has elected Stanisław Leszczyński king — a Pole and father-in-law of the French king Louis XV. But the neighbours want the Elector of Saxony, Augustus, on the throne. A Russian army enters the country, and the election is held again — for a different candidate.
level.leszczynski_1734.source: S. Leszczyński, Memoirs; J. Feldman, Poland in the Era of the War of the Polish Succession
level.leszczynski_1734.title: A King in Peasant Clothes
level.lokietek_cave.fact: Władysław the Elbow-high spent 1300–1304 in exile; according to local tradition, he hid in a cave near Ojców, and a spider covered the entrance with a web so that his pursuers decided no one was inside — it is now "Łokietek's Cave". Returning with Hungarian help, he spent twenty years gathering the lands, and on 20 January 1320 he was crowned in Kraków Cathedral by Archbishop Janisław — for the first time not in Gniezno but at Wawel, where almost all the kings of Poland were crowned from then on. This was the end of the fragmentation that began with Wrymouth's testament.
level.lokietek_cave.goal: A small duke hides from his pursuers in a cave, gathers supporters — and is crowned in Kraków, having reunited Poland
level.lokietek_cave.hint: Don't fight the pursuers one against many — first survive. A crown is not given to a fugitive: you need both strength and someone to place it on your head.
level.lokietek_cave.intro: The early 14th century. The Bohemian king Wenceslaus II has also become king of Poland, and the Kuyavian duke Władysław, nicknamed Łokietek for his small stature — "as tall as an elbow" — has been driven out. Bohemian troops are scouring Lesser Poland for him.
level.lokietek_cave.source: Jan Długosz, Annals, IX; Greater Poland Chronicle
level.lokietek_cave.title: Łokietek in the Cave
level.lublin_union.fact: On 1 March 1569 the Lithuanian magnates, led by Mikołaj Radziwiłł the Red, secretly left Lublin. The king responded by transferring Podlachia, Volhynia and then the Bracław and Kiev lands to the Crown, and the local nobility swore allegiance to the Crown. The Lithuanians returned, and on 1 July 1569 the union was signed: a common king, a common Sejm and currency, but a separate army, treasury, offices and laws for the Grand Duchy. Thus arose the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, the Commonwealth of Both Nations, which lasted until the partitions of 1795.
level.lublin_union.goal: The Lithuanian lords walk out of the Sejm, the king transfers part of their lands to the Crown — and two countries become one Commonwealth
level.lublin_union.hint: Persuasion won't convince the lords — they will leave anyway. What puts pressure on them is not the king but the loss of their lands. The union is signed by those who left.
level.lublin_union.intro: 1569, the Sejm in Lublin. The last Jagiellon, Sigismund Augustus, has no children, and the personal union of Poland and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania may end with his death. The Polish nobility wants a single state, the Lithuanian magnates want to keep their own. The Grand Duchy is at war with Muscovy and needs help.
level.lublin_union.source: Act of the Union of Lublin (1569); Diary of the Lublin Sejm
level.lublin_union.title: The Union of Lublin
level.maciejowice_1794.fact: On 10 October 1794 Kościuszko's army was defeated at Maciejowice; he himself, wounded, was captured and taken to St Petersburg. The phrase "Finis Poloniae!" — "The end of Poland!" — attributed to him was, according to his own letter of 1803, never spoken by him. On 4 November Suvorov's troops stormed Praga, a suburb of Warsaw; thousands of inhabitants were killed, and the capital capitulated. On 24 October 1795 the Third Partition wiped the Commonwealth off the map. Kościuszko, released in 1796, went to America, and in his will asked that the slaves of his friend Jefferson be freed — Jefferson did not carry out the wish.
level.maciejowice_1794.goal: The wounded Commander-in-Chief is taken prisoner, Warsaw capitulates — and a year later the Commonwealth vanishes from the map
level.maciejowice_1794.hint: The Commander-in-Chief did not flee the field. And, by his own letter, he never said the famous words "Finis Poloniae" — don't repeat the legend.
level.maciejowice_1794.intro: October 1794. The uprising has held out for half a year. Armies are marching on Warsaw from east and west. Kościuszko is trying to prevent the Russian corps of Fersen and Suvorov from joining up.
level.maciejowice_1794.source: T. Kościuszko, letter to Ségur (1803); J. U. Niemcewicz, Memoirs
level.maciejowice_1794.title: Maciejowice
level.malbork_1457.fact: The Order owed its mercenaries huge wages and gave them its castles as security. On 6 June 1457 the Bohemian captain Oldřich Červenka handed Malbork over to the Polish king for 190,000 Hungarian florins; Grand Master Ludwig von Erlichshausen left for Königsberg, which from then on became the Order's capital. The burghers of Malbork, led by Mayor Bartholomäus Blume, held the town for the Order for another three years — Blume was later executed. The war ended with the Second Peace of Toruń in 1466: Gdańsk Pomerania and Warmia passed to the Crown.
level.malbork_1457.goal: The Order cannot pay its mercenaries — and the king buys the Order's impregnable capital from them
level.malbork_1457.hint: Malbork cannot be taken by storm. But even the strongest fortress has a weak spot — the garrison has to be paid. You can only buy what already belongs to someone else.
level.malbork_1457.intro: 1457, the third year of the Thirteen Years' War. The Prussian towns have risen against the Teutonic Order and called in the Polish king Casimir IV Jagiellon. The king cannot take Malbork, the largest brick castle in Europe. But it is defended not by knights but by Bohemian mercenaries — and they have not been paid for a long time.
level.malbork_1457.source: Jan Długosz, Annals, XII; K. Górski, The Thirteen Years' War
level.malbork_1457.title: Malbork for Money
level.may3_1791.fact: On 3 May 1791, in the Royal Castle in Warsaw, the Sejm adopted the Constitution prepared by King Stanisław August, Hugo Kołłątaj, Ignacy Potocki and Marshal Stanisław Małachowski; the session was scheduled when many opponents had not yet returned from the Easter recess. It was the first written constitution of the modern type in Europe and the second in the world, after the American one: it abolished the liberum veto and the free election. It lasted fourteen months: its opponents formed the Targowica Confederation, called in the Russian army, and in 1793 the Second Partition followed. 3 May is a national holiday in Poland.
level.may3_1791.goal: The king and the reformers secretly write a constitution and pass it on a day when their opponents are still away for Easter
level.may3_1791.hint: If you wait until everyone has gathered, there will be no constitution. First the draft, then a convenient day, then the vote.
level.may3_1791.intro: 1788–1791, the Four-Year Sejm. After the First Partition the reformers want to save the state: abolish the liberum veto, make the throne hereditary, strengthen the army. Against them are the magnates who profit from the old order, and the neighbours.
level.may3_1791.title: The Constitution of 3 May
level.mazurek_1797.fact: In January 1797 the Polish Legions began to form in Milan. In July, in Reggio Emilia, Józef Wybicki wrote for them the "Song of the Polish Legions in Italy": "Poland has not yet perished, so long as we still live… March, march, Dąbrowski, from the Italian land to Poland." The song spread instantly, and in 1927 it became the national anthem — it still mentions Bonaparte. Some of the legionnaires were later sent to suppress the uprising in Haiti, and some went over to the Haitians' side — their descendants still live there.
level.mazurek_1797.goal: The Polish Legions gather in Italy under Bonaparte's banners — and a song is written for them that will become the anthem
level.mazurek_1797.hint: The song is for the army — so first the army. They have no home to return to: the state no longer exists.
level.mazurek_1797.intro: 1797. Poland is not on the map. General Jan Henryk Dąbrowski goes to the young General Bonaparte, who is defeating the Austrians in Italy, and asks permission to raise Polish legions — from émigrés and captured Poles who had served in the Austrian army.
level.mazurek_1797.source: J. Wybicki, Song of the Polish Legions (1797)
level.mazurek_1797.title: Dąbrowski's Mazurka
level.mieszko_baptism.fact: In 965 Mieszko married Dobrawa, daughter of the Bohemian duke Boleslaus I, and in 966 he was baptised — the exact date is unknown; by tradition it was Easter, 14 April. The German chronicler Thietmar of Merseburg writes that during the first Lent Dobrawa deliberately ate meat with her husband to win him over to the faith. Baptism through Bohemia rather than through the German bishoprics allowed Mieszko to avoid subordinating his church to Magdeburg, founded precisely in 968 to convert the Slavs. In that same year, 968, the first bishop appeared in Poznań — Jordan, subordinate, according to a widespread view, directly to Rome. The year 966 is considered the birth of the Polish state.
level.mieszko_baptism.goal: A pagan prince marries a Bohemian princess, is baptised through Prague rather than through the Germans — and gets his own bishop
level.mieszko_baptism.hint: The cross can be received from different hands. From the margrave's hands, a master comes along with the faith. First you need an alliance with Prague: a Bohemian bride — and Bohemian priests.
level.mieszko_baptism.intro: The mid-10th century. Mieszko, prince of the Polans, is a pagan, and for his neighbours that is a pretext: the German margraves call war against pagans a crusading cause. Margrave Hodo is already on the Oder. Mieszko will have to be baptised — the only question is by whom.
level.mieszko_baptism.source: Thietmar of Merseburg, Chronicle, IV, 55–56; Gallus Anonymus, I, 5; Annals of the Kraków Chapter
level.mieszko_baptism.title: The Baptism of Mieszko
level.november_11_1918.fact: On 10 November 1918 Piłsudski arrived in Warsaw by train. On 11 November — the day of the armistice on the Western Front — the Regency Council handed him supreme command of the army, and on 14 November it dissolved itself, handing over all power. German garrisons were disarmed by units of the Polish Military Organisation and volunteers, but mostly without a fight: the garrison's soldiers' council agreed to go home. Thus, after 123 years, Poland returned to the map; 11 November is Independence Day. Ahead lay years of wars over the borders — but that is another story.
level.november_11_1918.goal: The prisoner of Magdeburg returns to Warsaw, the Regency Council hands him power — and the German garrison leaves almost without a shot
level.november_11_1918.hint: He can only take command once he has returned. Power is not seized by storm — it is handed over. And the Germans are not stormed: they are disarmed and go home.
level.november_11_1918.intro: November 1918. Germany is losing the war, and there is revolution in Berlin. Warsaw is governed by the Regency Council, created by the Germans, and a German garrison is stationed in the city. In Magdeburg, Piłsudski is being released.
level.november_11_1918.source: Documents of the Regency Council, November 1918; memoirs of A. Skolimowski
level.november_11_1918.title: 11 November
level.oath_crisis_1917.fact: On 6 August 1914 the First Cadre Company marched out of Kraków. In July 1917 most of the legionnaires of the First and Third Brigades, following Piłsudski, refused to take the oath; on 22 July Governor-General Hans von Beseler ordered Piłsudski's arrest, and he spent more than a year in the fortress of Magdeburg. The arrest made him, in the eyes of Poles, a symbol of independence — one who had served none of the powers.
level.oath_crisis_1917.goal: The commander of the legions refuses to swear allegiance to the German emperor — and, as the prisoner of Magdeburg, becomes a hero
level.oath_crisis_1917.hint: First he needs the legions. Had he sworn, he would have become an officer of a foreign army — instead he became a prisoner.
level.oath_crisis_1917.intro: The First World War. In 1914 Józef Piłsudski led the First Cadre Company out of Kraków and created the Polish Legions, fighting on the side of Austria and Germany against Russia. In 1916 Germany and Austria proclaimed a "Kingdom of Poland" — without a king or borders. Now the legionnaires must swear an oath of "brotherhood in arms" with the armies of the Central Powers.
level.oath_crisis_1917.source: Documents of the 1917 Oath Crisis; J. Piłsudski, My First Battles
level.oath_crisis_1917.title: The Oath Crisis
level.odnowiciel_1039.fact: In 1038 or 1039 Bretislav sacked Gniezno and Poznań and carried off the relics of Saint Adalbert to Prague — Gniezno never recovered. In 1039 Casimir returned with a force that Gallus Anonymus puts at five hundred knights — help was provided by Emperor Henry III. The duke made Kraków, which had barely been touched by the devastation, the centre of the country — Kraków remained the capital until 1596. Casimir recovered Silesia only in 1050, and peace with Bohemia was concluded in 1054 through the emperor's mediation, in exchange for an annual tribute. The nickname "the Restorer" — Odnowiciel — was given to him by later historians.
level.odnowiciel_1039.goal: An exiled duke returns with knights obtained by his mother — and restores the country, making Kraków its capital
level.odnowiciel_1039.hint: Without help from abroad there is nothing to return with. Once back, don't rush to win back Silesia: first the country must be raised from the ruins, and a war with Bohemia now would lose even what remains.
level.odnowiciel_1039.intro: The 1030s. After the death of Mieszko II the Piast state collapsed: the pagans revolted, the nobles scattered, and the young Casimir was driven out. His mother Richeza, a niece of Emperor Otto III, lives in Germany. And the Bohemian duke Bretislav sees that Poland is defenceless.
level.odnowiciel_1039.source: Gallus Anonymus, I, 19; Cosmas of Prague, II, 2–5
level.odnowiciel_1039.title: Casimir the Restorer
level.olszynka_1831.fact: On 25 February 1831 at Olszynka Grochowska, Polish troops under General Chłopicki, who was severely wounded in the battle, held the grove all day, and Diebitsch abandoned the assault on Warsaw — the war lasted another half year. In September, during the storming of Warsaw, Redoubt No. 54 at Wola fell; Adam Mickiewicz wrote the ballad "Ordon's Redoubt", in which the artilleryman Julian Ordon blows it up together with himself. In reality Ordon survived, emigrated and died in 1887 — it is said that he read the ballad about his own death himself.
level.olszynka_1831.goal: The Polish army holds an alder grove outside Warsaw all day, and the artilleryman Ordon becomes a legend of the defence
level.olszynka_1831.hint: In the open field the field marshal's army is stronger — hold on to the grove. And Ordon's redoubt stands to the end, whatever was said about it later.
level.olszynka_1831.intro: February 1831. Field Marshal Diebitsch's army is marching on Warsaw to end the war with a single blow. Before the capital, near Grochów, there is an alder grove — Olszynka.
level.olszynka_1831.source: A. Mickiewicz, Ordon's Redoubt (1832); W. Tochowski, Memoirs
level.olszynka_1831.title: Olszynka and Ordon's Redoubt
level.paderewski_1918.fact: Paderewski gave hundreds of concerts and speeches in America for Poland's cause and became friends with Colonel Edward House, Wilson's closest adviser. On 8 January 1918, in Wilson's Fourteen Points, the thirteenth stated that an independent Polish state should be created with free and secure access to the sea. In 1919 Paderewski became prime minister and signed the Treaty of Versailles.
level.paderewski_1918.goal: A famous pianist, through his concerts and his friendship with the president's adviser, gets an independent Poland written into the peace programme
level.paderewski_1918.hint: Without fame no one would have listened to him. You don't go to the president directly, but through someone he trusts. And demanding borders right away would spoil everything.
level.paderewski_1918.intro: 1915–1917. Ignacy Paderewski is the most famous pianist in the world. He tours America giving concerts, raising money for starving Poland, and in every appearance speaks of Polish independence. President Woodrow Wilson is preparing a programme for the post-war peace.
level.paderewski_1918.source: W. Wilson, Fourteen Points (1918); diary of E. House
level.paderewski_1918.title: The Thirteenth Point
level.plowce_1331.fact: On 27 September 1331 at Płowce, Łokietek attacked a detachment of the Order that had fallen behind in the fog and defeated it; when the main forces arrived the battle ended in a draw, but for Poland it was the first field victory over the Teutonic Knights. According to the chroniclers, Prince Casimir was sent away from the field before the battle so as not to risk the heir. Płowce is linked to the legend of the knight Florian Szary: the king saw him with three spears in his body, holding in his spilled entrails — and supposedly this gave rise to the Jelita coat of arms with three spears.
level.plowce_1331.goal: The old king strikes a straggling column of the Order's knights, and the heir is led away from the field
level.plowce_1331.hint: The Order is strong as long as it marches as one army. First find where it has split. Keep the heir out of the fighting — he still has to rule.
level.plowce_1331.intro: 1331. The Teutonic Order, which has seized Gdańsk Pomerania, is sweeping through Kuyavia with fire. King Władysław the Elbow-high is over seventy, and his son Casimir is his only heir. The Order's army is larger than the Polish one.
level.plowce_1331.source: Jan Długosz, Annals, IX; Wigand of Marburg, Chronicle
level.plowce_1331.title: Płowce
level.polonium_1898.fact: In Paris Maria married the physicist Pierre Curie, and in 1898, in a cold shed on the rue Lhomond, they discovered two new elements. The first, announced in July 1898, she named polonium — "after the country of one of us". Radium was announced in December. In 1903 Skłodowska-Curie received the Nobel Prize in Physics, and in 1911 in Chemistry: she was the first person to win two Nobel Prizes. Her laboratory notebooks are still radioactive and are kept in lead boxes.
level.polonium_1898.goal: A Warsaw woman who studied in secret discovers a new element in Paris and names it after a country that is not on the map
level.polonium_1898.hint: She arrives in Paris already a student of the underground university. Radium was not announced first — the name of the first element was a political gesture.
level.polonium_1898.intro: 1891. Maria Skłodowska is twenty-four. In Warsaw, under imperial rule, university is closed to women, and she studies at the underground "Flying University", which moves from apartment to apartment. Now she is going to Paris, to the Sorbonne.
level.polonium_1898.source: M. and P. Curie, communication to the Academy of Sciences, July 1898
level.polonium_1898.title: Polonium
level.poniatowski_1764.fact: Poniatowski was Catherine's lover in 1755–1758. On 7 September 1764 he was elected king while Russian troops stood near Warsaw; Catherine wrote that she had "made" him king. In 1767–1768 the Russian ambassador Nikolai Repnin arrested and exiled to Kaluga Bishops Sołtyk and Załuski and Hetman Rzewuski, who had opposed him, and forced the Sejm to pass laws under Russia's guarantee. Stanisław August was an intelligent, educated king and patron of the arts — and he reigned over a country that less and less governed itself.
level.poniatowski_1764.goal: The empress's former lover becomes King of Poland — and discovers that her ambassador will rule in his place
level.poniatowski_1764.hint: First the romance, then the crown. He dreamed of marrying the empress, but it never happened. A king by patronage signs what he is dictated.
level.poniatowski_1764.intro: 1755, St Petersburg. A young Polish aristocrat, Stanisław Poniatowski, serves as secretary to the British ambassador and falls in love with Grand Duchess Catherine. Nine years later she is empress, and Poland is electing a king.
level.poniatowski_1764.source: Memoirs of Stanisław August; letters of Catherine II
level.poniatowski_1764.title: A King by Patronage
level.popiel_piast.fact: Prince Popiel was cruel: legend has it that he poisoned his uncles at a feast and left their bodies unburied. When two wanderers came to the prince's feast for the first haircut of his son, they were driven from the courtyard. The wanderers knocked at the cottage of the poor wheelwright Piast and his wife Rzepicha — they too were celebrating, the first haircut of their son Siemowit, but there was only food enough for one table. Piast welcomed the guests like family — and then a miracle happened: the keg of mead and the piece of pork in his cottage kept growing and growing, until there was enough to feed even the prince's guests. The wanderers cut Siemowit's hair and foretold that he would be prince. And punishment overtook Popiel: from the bodies of the poisoned uncles came swarms of mice, which drove the prince into a tower above Lake Gopło and devoured him. The people chose Siemowit as their prince — and with him began the Piast dynasty, which ruled Poland for more than four hundred years.
level.popiel_piast.goal: A cruel prince drives wanderers from his feast, a poor wheelwright takes them in — and his son becomes prince, while Popiel is eaten by mice
level.popiel_piast.hint: The wanderers come to the prince first — they go to the wheelwright only after being driven away. Piast is no conspirator: it was hospitality, not rebellion, that made his family princes. And Popiel will be dealt with without human hands.
level.popiel_piast.intro: In Gniezno rules Prince Popiel — cruel and, rumour has it, the poisoner of his uncles. He is holding a feast: the young prince is having his hair cut for the first time, the ritual of postrzyżyny, after which a boy becomes a man. Two wanderers come to the town. In the outer settlement, the wheelwright Piast and his wife Rzepka are also holding a haircutting — for their son Siemowit — but the poor have food for only one table.
level.popiel_piast.source: Gallus Anonymus, The Deeds of the Princes of the Poles, I, 1–3; Wincenty Kadłubek, Chronicle
level.popiel_piast.title: Popiel and the Mice
level.prussian_homage.fact: On 10 April 1525, in the Main Market Square of Kraków, Albrecht knelt before Sigismund the Old and received Prussia as a fief, as a hereditary duchy. Thus appeared the first Protestant state in Europe — and the former Teutonic Order became a Polish vassal. The irony of history: in 1657 Albrecht's descendants freed themselves from vassalage, and a century later Prussia took part in the partitions of Poland. Jan Matejko painted "The Prussian Homage" in 1882, when Poland was not on the map.
level.prussian_homage.goal: The last Grand Master of the Teutonic Order dissolves the Order and, in a Kraków square, swears allegiance to the Polish king as a vassal
level.prussian_homage.hint: The Grand Master of a monastic order cannot become anyone's vassal — first he will have to stop being Grand Master. And finishing him off on the battlefield means years more of war.
level.prussian_homage.intro: 1525. The last war with the Order has ended in a truce. Grand Master Albrecht Hohenzollern — nephew of the Polish king Sigismund the Old — has visited Luther, who advised him to marry and turn the Order into a secular duchy.
level.prussian_homage.source: Treaty of Kraków, 1525; Justus Ludwik Decius, On the Times of Sigismund
level.prussian_homage.title: The Prussian Homage
level.psie_pole.fact: Gallus Anonymus, a contemporary of the events, relates that Bolesław forbade the people of Głogów to surrender, and when the truce ended the emperor had the hostages, the townspeople's children, tied to the siege engines — but the defenders beat off the assault all the same. The siege failed, and Henry's army, worn down by guerrilla warfare, withdrew. The battle of Psie Pole ("Dogs' Field") near Wrocław on 24 August 1109 is first mentioned by Wincenty Kadłubek a century later: supposedly the field was so named for the dogs that dragged away the corpses — this is more likely a legend, as Gallus is silent about a great battle. He does, however, quote a mocking song sung about the Germans: "Poland cannot be taken with gold."
level.psie_pole.goal: The townspeople of Głogów do not surrender even when the emperor ties their children to the siege engines — and the duke strikes the weakened army
level.psie_pole.hint: While the emperor is at full strength, he cannot be beaten in the field. The town will hold only if it knows the duke's will — without it, it will surrender. And no peace: the emperor left empty-handed.
level.psie_pole.intro: 1109. Emperor Henry V marches on Poland to put Bolesław Wrymouth's exiled brother, Zbigniew, on the throne. First in his path stands Głogów on the Oder. The townspeople begged a five-day truce and gave hostages, promising to surrender if the duke did not come.
level.psie_pole.source: Gallus Anonymus, III, 5–15; Wincenty Kadłubek, Chronicle, III
level.psie_pole.title: Głogów and Psie Pole
level.somosierra_1808.fact: On Napoleon's order, the third squadron of the Polish chevau-légers under Jan Kozietulski charged up the gorge, about two and a half kilometres long, and took all four batteries in seven or eight minutes. Kozietulski's horse was killed under him at the start of the charge; the last battery was taken by the wounded Lieutenant Andrzej Niegolewski. The charge is credited with the cry "Forward, you sons of dogs, the Emperor is watching!" The road to Madrid was open, and Napoleon awarded the squadron crosses of the Legion of Honour.
level.somosierra_1808.goal: In eight minutes a Polish squadron sweeps through four Spanish batteries in a mountain gorge — and opens the road to Madrid for Napoleon
level.somosierra_1808.hint: A detour through the mountains seems sensible — but the army would lose a day. The charge is impossible until it is ordered.
level.somosierra_1808.intro: 30 November 1808, Spain. The road to Madrid is blocked by the Somosierra gorge: four batteries of Spanish artillery on the winding road. Napoleon's infantry is stuck. Beside the emperor is a squadron of the Polish light horse — the chevau-légers of the Guard.
level.somosierra_1808.source: Reports of the Grande Armée, 1808; A. Niegolewski, A Few Words on Somosierra
level.somosierra_1808.title: Somosierra
level.stanislaus_1079.fact: Bishop Stanislaus was executed on 11 April 1079 by the king's sentence — Gallus Anonymus calls him a "traitor" without explaining what the treason was. According to a later Life, the king himself cut the bishop down at the altar of the church on Skałka and had the body hacked to pieces. The killing roused the nobility: Bolesław fled to Hungary and died in exile around 1081, and his brother Władysław Herman ruled — now as a duke, without a crown. In 1253 Stanislaus was canonised, and according to legend the dismembered body miraculously grew back together — this came to be seen as a sign that fragmented Poland would one day be united again. He is a patron saint of Poland, and kings made a penitential pilgrimage to his tomb at Wawel before their coronation.
level.stanislaus_1079.goal: The king executes the bishop — and the slain bishop topples the king: the nobility drives him out and puts his brother on the throne
level.stanislaus_1079.hint: The king will not make peace — otherwise there would be neither martyr nor revolt. The revolt cannot be crushed: the king is overthrown not by the sword but by what he did. And the brother is not put on the throne by the brothers themselves.
level.stanislaus_1079.intro: 1079. Bolesław the Bold — a king who has fought from Kiev to Prague — rules harshly. Stanislaus, Bishop of Kraków, opposes him, and the king accuses him of treason. The nobility harbours a grudge: the king is too autocratic.
level.stanislaus_1079.source: Gallus Anonymus, I, 27; Wincenty of Kielcza, Life of Saint Stanislaus (13th century)
level.stanislaus_1079.title: The Bishop on Skałka
level.teutonic_call.fact: In 1226 Konrad of Masovia invited the Teutonic Order and gave it the Chełmno Land. Grand Master Hermann von Salza, a skilful diplomat, obtained that same year from Emperor Frederick II the Golden Bull of Rimini, recognising all the Order's future conquests in Prussia — Konrad probably did not know of it. The knights arrived in 1230 and within half a century, by 1283, had subdued the Prussians, building on their land their own state with castles from Toruń to Königsberg. For two hundred years it would be Poland's main enemy — until Grunwald and the Thirteen Years' War — and in 1525 it would become the Duchy of Prussia, from which the Kingdom of Prussia would grow.
level.teutonic_call.goal: A duke who cannot cope with the Prussian raids calls in German knights — and, having subdued the Prussians, they build their own state on their land
level.teutonic_call.hint: The duke cannot defeat the Prussians on his own. The knights do not come for free — they need land, and land is given by the one ruined by the raids.
level.teutonic_call.intro: The 13th century. Poland is fragmented into provinces. Year after year Duke Konrad of Masovia fends off the pagan Prussians who burn his borderland — and he is losing. He has already founded his own knightly order, the Brothers of Dobrzyń, but it failed. In the south, in Hungary, another order has just been left without land — the German one, the Teutonic Order.
level.teutonic_call.source: Golden Bull of Rimini (1226); Peter of Dusburg, Chronicle of the Prussian Land
level.teutonic_call.title: Calling In the Order
level.twardowski.fact: The nobleman Twardowski wanted to know everything hidden from mortals. One night on Krzemionki, across the Vistula, he summoned the devil and signed a pact in blood: the devil would serve him in all things, but would take his soul only when Twardowski found himself in Rome. Twardowski flew on a rooster, galloped on a painted horse, showed the king his dead wife in a magic mirror — and for many years he steered well clear of Rome. But one day he stepped into a roadside inn, not knowing it was called "Rome". The devil appeared, seized him and carried him up into the sky. Then Twardowski began to sing a hymn to the Mother of God that he had sung as a boy — and the devil let him slip from his claws. Twardowski got stuck on the Moon and sits there to this day, and his only friend, a little spider, lowers itself to earth on a thread and brings him news.
level.twardowski.goal: A Kraków nobleman sells his soul to the devil on condition that it be taken only in Rome — and is caught in an inn called "Rome"
level.twardowski.hint: Without a pact the devil has nothing to take. Twardowski won't go to the real Rome — he is caught where he least expects it. And it is a song that saves him, not cunning.
level.twardowski.intro: The 16th century, Kraków. The learned nobleman Twardowski craves knowledge and power over nature. At night on Krzemionki, the limestone hills across the Vistula, he summons the devil.
level.twardowski.source: Polish folk legends; A. Mickiewicz, Pani Twardowska (1822)
level.twardowski.title: Pan Twardowski
level.varna_1444.fact: On 10 November 1444 at Varna on the Black Sea coast, Władysław, against John Hunyadi's advice to hold the line, attacked the Janissaries at the sultan's headquarters with five hundred knights and was killed; according to tradition, Murad sent his head to Bursa in a jar of honey. It is said that the sultan had the charter of the broken peace raised on a spear like a banner. The king's body was never found — and so legends long circulated that he had survived; one of them made him the Portuguese knight Henrique Alemão on Madeira. Nine years later Constantinople fell.
level.varna_1444.goal: The young king swears peace to the sultan, breaks the oath — and dies attacking the sultan's tent
level.varna_1444.hint: You can only break an oath you have sworn. Hunyadi holds the line — but he is not the one who decides the campaign. The battle's fate was decided by the king's impulse.
level.varna_1444.intro: 1444. Władysław III, King of Poland and Hungary, is twenty years old. In the summer, at Szeged, he swears a ten-year peace to Sultan Murad II. But the pope and Venice promise a fleet, the cardinal-legate Cesarini says an oath to infidels is not binding, and the crusade goes on.
level.varna_1444.source: Jan Długosz, Annals, XII; Callimachus, History of King Władysław
level.varna_1444.title: Varna
level.veto_1652.fact: On 9 March 1652 the envoy from Upytė, Władysław Siciński, lodged a protest against extending the Sejm and left; Marshal Andrzej Maksymilian Fredro acknowledged that without everyone's consent the Sejm could not continue. It was said that Siciński had been bribed by the Lithuanian magnate Janusz Radziwiłł. It was the first Sejm broken up by a single vote — the liberum veto. In the following hundred-odd years nearly half of all Sejms ended this way, and the state almost lost the ability to make decisions. According to legend, Siciński's body did not decay after his death, and for a long time the "accursed" man was displayed in the church in Upytė.
level.veto_1652.goal: One envoy shouts "Nie pozwalam!" — and the entire Sejm of the Commonwealth is dissolved without a single decision
level.veto_1652.hint: You can only break up a Sejm whose term has expired and which has to be extended unanimously. And the "Nie pozwalam" isn't shouted for nothing — there is money behind it. If the king talks the envoy round, nothing will happen — but it did.
level.veto_1652.intro: 1652. In the Commonwealth, decisions of the Sejm are taken unanimously: every nobleman is equal to every other. Until now dissenters have been persuaded — or shouted down. The Sejm in Warsaw has been sitting for six weeks, and its term is running out.
level.veto_1652.source: Diary of the Sejm of 1652; W. Konopczyński, Liberum Veto
level.veto_1652.title: Liberum Veto
level.vienna_1683.fact: In August Jerzy Kulczycki, who knew Turkish, passed through the besiegers' camp and back in Turkish clothes, carrying letters. On 12 September 1683 Sobieski led the combined army down from the hills of the Kahlenberg; the charge of about eighteen thousand horsemen, among them several thousand winged hussars, is considered the largest cavalry charge in history. The vizier fled, abandoning his camp; in December he was strangled in Belgrade on the sultan's orders. Sobieski wrote to the pope: "Venimus, vidimus, Deus vicit" — "We came, we saw, God conquered." Legend credits Kulczycki with the first Viennese coffee house, using captured beans; in fact the first was opened by the Armenian Johannes Diodato in 1685.
level.vienna_1683.goal: A spy carries word through the Turkish camp, King John III leads an army to the rescue — and the winged hussars charge down the hill and save Vienna
level.vienna_1683.hint: The king won't come until he knows. The emperor has left Vienna, and a sortie is beyond him. The charge from the hill decides it.
level.vienna_1683.intro: Summer 1683. Grand Vizier Kara Mustafa with a huge Ottoman army is besieging Vienna, the capital of the Habsburg empire. Emperor Leopold I has left for Passau. The city is holding on with its last strength. The Polish king John III Sobieski has promised to come to its aid — but for that someone must get through the Turkish camp.
level.vienna_1683.source: John III Sobieski, letters to Marysieńka (1683); F. Kollonitsch; Diary of the Siege of Vienna
level.vienna_1683.title: Vienna
level.walewska_1807.fact: According to Walewska's memoirs, Polish patriots persuaded her that her favour towards the emperor was a duty to her homeland. On 7 July 1807, by the Peace of Tilsit, Napoleon created the Duchy of Warsaw — with a constitution and an army, but not a kingdom; Prince Józef Poniatowski became minister of war. In 1810 Walewska gave birth to a son, Alexandre, later French foreign minister. That same year the emperor married Marie Louise of Austria. Walewska visited him on Elba.
level.walewska_1807.goal: Patriots persuade a young countess to become Napoleon's lover for Poland's sake — and the emperor creates the Duchy of Warsaw
level.walewska_1807.hint: The countess did not seek this love herself — she was asked. The emperor did not marry her: his wife was chosen from the Habsburgs. And the duchy was won not for love, but through it.
level.walewska_1807.intro: January 1807, Warsaw. Napoleon has crushed Prussia, and the Poles hope he will restore their state. At a ball the emperor notices eighteen-year-old Countess Maria Walewska, wife of an elderly chamberlain.
level.walewska_1807.source: Memoirs of M. Walewska; Peace of Tilsit, 1807
level.walewska_1807.title: Madame Walewska
level.wanda.fact: After Prince Krak died, his daughter Wanda came to rule in Kraków — so beautiful and wise that her fame reached the German lands. Prince Rytygier sent matchmakers, and when he was refused, he came with an army to take both the princess and her land by force. Wanda herself rode out at the head of her warriors to meet the enemy. But when Rytygier's soldiers saw her, they lowered their weapons and refused to fight her. Abandoned by his army, Rytygier in despair threw himself on his own sword. And Wanda, as another version of the tale goes, so that no one would ever shed blood over her again, offered herself to the gods and threw herself into the Vistula. Over her grave the people raised a mound — it still stands near Kraków today.
level.wanda.goal: A princess refuses a foreign suitor and rides out to face his army — and the army refuses to fight her
level.wanda.hint: A wedding is not for Wanda, and in the field her army is weaker. Her weapon is herself: first the refusal, then to ride out and face the foreign army.
level.wanda.intro: After the death of Kraków's founder, Prince Krak, his daughter Wanda took the throne — so beautiful and wise that her fame reached the German lands. Rytygier, prince of the Alemanni, sent matchmakers. And when he was refused, he brought an army.
level.wanda.source: Wincenty Kadłubek, Chronicle, I, 7; Jan Długosz, Annals, I
level.wanda.title: Wanda, Who Would Not Wed a German
level.warsaw_confederation.fact: On 28 January 1573 the Warsaw Confederation proclaimed: "we who differ in religion will keep the peace among ourselves" — for the first time in Europe, freedom of worship for the nobility was enshrined in law; only one of the bishops signed the act. In May Henry of Valois was elected king. When, in Notre-Dame Cathedral, he hesitated to swear to the religious peace, the Polish envoy told him: "Si non iurabis, non regnabis" — "If you do not swear, you will not reign." The act of the Confederation is listed in UNESCO's Memory of the World Register.
level.warsaw_confederation.goal: The nobility swears not to wage war over faith and forces the new king, brother of the man behind the St Bartholomew's Day Massacre, to swear to this peace
level.warsaw_confederation.hint: First peace between the faiths — then the election, or they will elect someone who will break it. The primate will try to talk the marshal into backing down; don't give in.
level.warsaw_confederation.intro: 1573. The last Jagiellon is dead, and for the first time the king will be elected by the whole nobility. Among Catholics, Lutherans, Calvinists and Orthodox, it is frightening to recall that half a year ago in Paris, on St Bartholomew's night, Catholics slaughtered thousands of Protestants. The leading candidate is the French prince Henry of Valois, brother of the king who arranged that night.
level.warsaw_confederation.source: Act of the Warsaw Confederation (1573); Henrician Articles
level.warsaw_confederation.title: The Warsaw Confederation
level.warsaw_mermaid.fact: Two mermaid sisters swam in from the sea: one stayed by the shores of Denmark, while the other swam up the Vistula to a small fishing village. At night the fishermen would find their nets tangled and their fish set free, and they resolved to catch the mischief-maker. But when they heard her song over the river, their hands dropped — so beautifully did she sing. Then a sly, rich merchant caught the mermaid and locked her in a wooden shed, meaning to cart her around the fairs and charge money to see her. That night a young fisherman named Wars heard her weeping and, with his friends, set her free. The grateful mermaid swore to protect their town whenever danger threatened it. That is why the Warsaw Mermaid holds a sword and a shield — she guards Warsaw to this day.
level.warsaw_mermaid.goal: A greedy merchant catches a mermaid, a poor fisherman frees her — and the mermaid takes up a sword to defend the city
level.warsaw_mermaid.hint: For the mermaid to be saved, she must first be caught. Only someone who took no money will free her. And she gives her oath to her rescuer.
level.warsaw_mermaid.intro: On the bank of the Vistula stands a small fishing village. At night the fishermen hear wondrous singing over the river — and see that someone is tearing their nets. One day a wealthy merchant passing through hears the song too.
level.warsaw_mermaid.source: Warsaw city legends; S. Kwiatkowski, Warsaw Legends
level.warsaw_mermaid.title: The Warsaw Mermaid
level.wawel_dragon.fact: A dragon made its lair in a cave beneath Wawel Hill. At first it devoured the cattle, then it began demanding people, and Kraków lived in fear. Prince Krak promised his daughter's hand to whoever rid the city of the monster — and knights in gleaming armour went to the cave one after another, but none returned. Then a poor shoemaker named Skuba took a ram, stuffed its hide with sulphur and pitch, sewed it up and left it by the cave. The dragon swallowed it whole — and a fire blazed up in its belly. The monster rushed to the Vistula and drank, and drank, and drank, until it burst. Skuba won the princess as his bride, and the cave — the Smocza Jama, the Dragon's Den — can still be seen beneath Wawel; at its entrance stands a dragon that breathes real fire.
level.wawel_dragon.goal: Knights perish in the dragon's cave, but a simple shoemaker tosses it a ram full of sulphur — and the dragon drinks the Vistula until it bursts
level.wawel_dragon.hint: The dragon can't be beaten by force — it eats knights. Cunning is needed, and cunning has to be prepared first. The reward goes to the one who won.
level.wawel_dragon.intro: A dragon has settled beneath Wawel Hill. It devours cattle, and then people, and Prince Krak promises a generous reward to whoever rids the city of the monster. Knights in armour go to the cave one after another.
level.wawel_dragon.source: Wincenty Kadłubek, Chronicle, I, 5; Marcin Bielski, Polish Chronicle (16th century)
level.wawel_dragon.title: The Wawel Dragon
level.wierzynek_1364.fact: On 12 May 1364 Casimir founded a university in Kraków — the future Jagiellonian University, the second in Central Europe after Prague. In September the Congress of Kraków brought together Emperor Charles IV, Louis of Hungary, Peter of Cyprus, Valdemar of Denmark and German princes; Casimir reconciled Charles with Louis. According to Długosz, the guests were entertained by the wealthy Kraków merchant Wierzynek — and the Wierzynek restaurant on the Main Market Square still dates itself from 1364. Of Casimir, Długosz would say: "he found Poland wooden and left it brick."
level.wierzynek_1364.goal: The king founds a university, and at a feast hosted by a Kraków merchant he reconciles the emperor with the King of Hungary
level.wierzynek_1364.hint: The king founded the university in spring, before the congress. It is easier to reconcile guests at the table than on the battlefield — but first you need a table. And don't let the guests come to blows before they sit down.
level.wierzynek_1364.intro: 1364. Casimir the Great, the last of the Piasts, has turned a ruined country into a power to be reckoned with. Emperor Charles IV and King Louis of Hungary are quarrelling: the emperor insulted Louis's mother — Casimir's sister. Kings are converging on Kraków.
level.wierzynek_1364.source: Jan Długosz, Annals, IX; Jan of Czarnków, Chronicle
level.wierzynek_1364.title: The Feast at Wierzynek's
level.wrzesnia_1901.fact: In the spring of 1901 the schoolchildren of Września refused to answer in German in religion lessons; they were punished with the rod. On 20 May the parents burst into the school; in the autumn a court in Gniezno sentenced dozens of adults to prison, the mother of one of the pupils to two and a half years. Newspapers all over Europe wrote about Września, and Henryk Sienkiewicz and Maria Konopnicka spoke out in defence of the children. In 1906–1907 a school strike involved, by various estimates, up to seventy-five thousand children in the Prussian part of Poland.
level.wrzesnia_1901.goal: Schoolchildren refuse to pray in German, they are flogged — and their mothers' protest echoes across Europe
level.wrzesnia_1901.hint: If the mother persuades her son to give in, nothing will happen — but it did. The parents' protest began with the rods.
level.wrzesnia_1901.intro: 1901, the town of Września in Greater Poland, part of Prussia. The Polish language is being squeezed out of the schools; now even religious instruction must be learned and answered in German, from German catechisms.
level.wrzesnia_1901.source: Records of the 1901 Gniezno trial; M. Konopnicka, Rota
level.wrzesnia_1901.title: The Children of Września
