level.vistulans_880.title: Prince of the Vistulans
level.vistulans_880.goal: Methodius warns a pagan prince on the Vistula. The prince laughs, and the prophecy comes true: he will be baptised as a captive
level.vistulans_880.hint: The advice was given, but history did not follow it. A prince baptised of his own free will would never have been taken captive, and we need things as they were.
level.vistulans_880.intro: Around 880. On the upper Vistula, where Kraków will one day stand, a mighty pagan prince rules the Vistulans. To the south Great Moravia of Prince Svatopluk is growing, and there the Slavic teacher Methodius is preaching: the man who, with his brother Cyril, gave the Slavs their alphabet.
level.vistulans_880.fact: The Life of Methodius tells how a pagan prince “on the Vistula” mistreated Christians, and Methodius sent word to him: “It would be good for you, my son, to be baptised of your own will on your own land, lest you be baptised by force as a captive in a foreign land; and then you will remember me.” The prince did not listen. Soon Svatopluk of Moravia conquered the Vistulans, and, the Life says, the prince was indeed baptised in captivity. This is the first mention in written sources of the lands of future Lesser Poland, almost a century before the baptism of Mieszko.
level.chrobry_crown_1025.title: The First King
level.chrobry_crown_1025.goal: Bolesław the Brave waits twenty-five years for a crown, and puts it on the moment the emperor dies
level.chrobry_crown_1025.hint: Asking the emperor is pointless: he will say “no”, and it will be remembered. Sometimes the best move is to wait.
level.chrobry_crown_1025.intro: 1024. Bolesław the Brave is the strongest ruler between the Elbe and the Dnieper: he fought Emperor Henry II for fifteen years and never lost. A royal crown was promised to him back in 1000 at Gniezno, but Henry will never allow it. Bolesław is nearly sixty.
level.chrobry_crown_1025.fact: On 13 July 1024 Henry II died without a son, and the empire began electing a new king. While the Germans had no time for Poland, at Easter 1025 the archbishop in Gniezno crowned Bolesław, the first King of Poland. He reigned as king for only two months and died on 17 June 1025. A German chronicler wrote with irritation that Bolesław had “usurped” the crown; he was succeeded by his son Mieszko II, crowned that same year.
level.chrobry_crown_1025.source: Annals of Quedlinburg; Gallus Anonymus, Deeds of the Princes of the Poles
level.magdeburg_1257.title: Kraków Under Magdeburg Law
level.magdeburg_1257.goal: After the Mongol fire, Kraków is rebuilt from scratch under German law, with self-government and a vast Market Square
level.magdeburg_1257.hint: A town is people, but not just any people: the duke has his own peasants and had no intention of giving them up. You lay out a square once there are people to trade in it.
level.magdeburg_1257.intro: 1257. Sixteen years ago the Mongols burned Kraków to the ground. Duke Bolesław the Chaste wants the capital of Lesser Poland to rise again quickly and richly, and he summons three wójts to build the city on the model of German towns.
level.magdeburg_1257.fact: On 5 June 1257 Bolesław the Chaste granted the wójts Gedko, Jakub and Dytmar a charter: Kraków received Magdeburg law, with its own court, a town council and liberties for the burghers. In the middle of the city a Market Square was laid out, about 200 by 200 metres and one of the largest medieval squares in Europe, surrounded by a grid of straight streets that survives to this day. The charter had a crafty clause: the wójts were forbidden to admit the duke's peasants to the city, because the duke did not want to lose his subjects or their taxes. From there Magdeburg law spread across Poland: by the 16th century hundreds of towns lived under it.
level.kalisz_1264.title: The Statute of Kalisz
level.kalisz_1264.goal: The Duke of Greater Poland places the Jews under the protection of the law, and for centuries Poland becomes home to the largest Jewish community in the world
level.kalisz_1264.hint: A community rests on the law, not the other way round. Slander builds nothing; it only destroys.
level.kalisz_1264.intro: 1264. Terrible libels against the Jews are spreading across Europe, and they are expelled from one town after another. The Duke of Greater Poland, Bolesław the Pious, does the opposite and invites them into his towns: he needs trade, money and crafts.
level.kalisz_1264.fact: On 16 August 1264 in Kalisz, Bolesław the Pious issued a statute: a Jew was to be judged by the duke, not by the mob; killing a Jew meant death and confiscation; no one could accuse Jews of using Christian blood, and a Christian who made such a charge and failed to prove it suffered the same penalty. The statute even had a touching clause: if a Jew cried for help at night and his Christian neighbours did not come, they paid a fine. Casimir the Great extended the statute to the whole kingdom, and over several centuries hundreds of thousands of Jews settled in Poland. In 1580 the communities even received their own “parliament”, the Council of Four Lands.
level.kalisz_1264.source: Statute of Kalisz of Bolesław the Pious, 1264
level.academy_1400.title: The Queen's Jewels
level.academy_1400.goal: The dying Jadwiga leaves her jewels to the university, and Jagiełło revives the Kraków Academy
level.academy_1400.hint: The king has only one treasury, and the temptation to spend it on war with the Order is great. Without the will there is nothing to open.
level.academy_1400.intro: 1399. The university founded by Casimir the Great has almost faded away since his death. Queen Jadwiga dreams of reviving it, but she is gravely ill after childbirth. War with the Teutonic Order draws ever closer, and the lords count every coin.
level.academy_1400.fact: Jadwiga died on 17 July 1399 and bequeathed her jewels to the revival of the academy. On 26 July 1400 Jagiełło reopened it in a house bought from the Pęcherz family of burghers, today the Collegium Maius; its first rector was Stanislaus of Skarbimierz, and the first speech was a sermon on the value of learning. A hundred years later Nicolaus Copernicus would study here. Today it is the Jagiellonian University, one of the oldest in Europe.
level.academy_1400.source: Jan Długosz, Annals, under 1399–1400; Jagiełło's charter of 26 July 1400
level.nihil_novi_1505.title: Nihil novi
level.nihil_novi_1505.goal: The Sejm at Radom decides that the king can introduce nothing new without the nobility's consent, and noble democracy is born
level.nihil_novi_1505.hint: The lords will offer the king an easy path: rule by the few. The nobility's voice must first be chosen back home in the province.
level.nihil_novi_1505.intro: 1505. King Alexander Jagiellon is squeezed between powerful magnates and a numerous nobility. Four years ago the magnates wrung the Privilege of Mielnik from him: all power to the Senate. Now the nobility, about a tenth of the population, demands its share.
level.nihil_novi_1505.fact: On 30 May 1505 the Sejm at Radom passed the constitution “Nihil novi nisi commune consensu”, “nothing new without common consent”: the king could not make laws without the Senate and the Chamber of Deputies. The Privilege of Mielnik never came into force. In 1506 Chancellor Jan Łaski published the first printed code of Polish law, Łaski's Statute, with an engraving of the king in the Sejm. Noble democracy was unique in Europe: a tenth of the country could vote, many times more than in France or England at the time. Its shadow was the peasantry, which had no vote at all.
level.rej_1562.title: Poles Are Not Geese
level.rej_1562.goal: Mikołaj Rej, a nobleman with poor Latin, starts writing in Polish and becomes “the father of Polish literature”
level.rej_1562.hint: Learned advice is not always useful: Latin will lead the book away from its reader. The nobleman will be the one reading, so write for him.
level.rej_1562.intro: The 16th century. Educated Poland speaks and writes in Latin: laws, science, theology and poetry are all in Latin. Mikołaj Rej of Nagłowice is a self-taught nobleman who never properly learned Latin. But he knows how people talk at the market, in the tavern and on the manor.
level.rej_1562.fact: Rej wrote only in Polish: satires, sermons, moral tales, The Life of an Honest Man. In 1562, in his collection The Menagerie, he left a line every Polish schoolchild knows: “let the neighbouring nations know that Poles are not geese, they have a tongue of their own” (the honking of geese being a jibe at Latin). Alongside him worked Jan Kochanowski, the first great poet of the Polish language: in 1580 he published the Laments, a lament for his two-year-old daughter Urszula, and for the first time in Poland private grief became high poetry.
level.rej_1562.source: Mikołaj Rej, The Menagerie (1562); Jan Kochanowski, Laments (1580)
level.grain_gdansk.title: The Granary of Europe
level.grain_gdansk.goal: Polish rye floats down the Vistula to Gdańsk and on to Amsterdam: the nobility's wealth rests on the serf
level.grain_gdansk.hint: Grain does not grow by itself: first someone has to work the lord's field. If the peasant runs away, there will be nothing to sell.
level.grain_gdansk.intro: The 16th century. The Netherlands and Western Europe are growing and need bread. Poland has black soil and the Vistula, which flows straight to Gdańsk. The nobleman realises it pays better not to collect rent from his peasants but to sow for the market himself, with those same peasants' hands.
level.grain_gdansk.fact: In 1496 the Sejm forbade peasants to leave their villages freely, and the Statute of Toruń of 1520 imposed compulsory labour service, one day a week; by the 17th century it reached three to six days. The lords' folwark estates sent rye down the Vistula on rafts and szkuta barges; the raftsmen, the flisaks, were called “Vistula sailors”. Gdańsk became the largest port on the Baltic, and the Dutch called the Baltic grain trade “the mother of all trades”. The nobility grew rich and built palaces, while peasants fled the labour service to the borderlands and the Dnieper steppes.
level.grain_gdansk.source: Statute of Toruń (1520); M. Małowist, East and West Europe in the 13th–16th Centuries
level.batory_1579.title: King of Men, Not of Consciences
level.batory_1579.goal: Stephen Báthory gives the Jesuits a university in Vilnius, yet lets no one be persecuted for their faith
level.batory_1579.hint: The king must first become king, and the condition of the election is known. A zealous preacher is dangerous to someone nobody protected.
level.batory_1579.intro: 1576. After Henry of Valois flees, the nobility elects the Transylvanian prince Stephen Báthory, on condition that he marry Anna Jagiellon, sister of the last Jagiellon. He is a Catholic who favours the Jesuits, and the Jesuit Piotr Skarga is the finest preacher in the land. But all around are Calvinists, Lutherans and Orthodox, and everyone remembers the oath of the Warsaw Confederation.
level.batory_1579.fact: On 1 May 1576 Báthory married Anna and was crowned on the same day. He supported the Jesuits: on 1 April 1579 he raised their college in Vilnius to an academy, the first university of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, with Piotr Skarga as its first rector. Yet he firmly kept the peace between faiths. He is credited with the words: “I am king of men, not of consciences.” The Calvinist Mikołaj Radziwiłł the Red remained his hetman and chancellor of Lithuania. The Vilnius Academy is today Vilnius University.
level.batory_1579.source: Stephen Báthory's privilege for the Vilnius Academy (1579); R. Heidenstein, Commentaries on the Muscovite War
level.arians_1658.title: The Expulsion of the Polish Brethren
level.arians_1658.goal: A country that swore not to persecute for faith expels the Arians, and their books, printed in Amsterdam, change the thinking of Europe
level.arians_1658.hint: You can stay only by renouncing your faith, and then there will be no book. They will print where no one is persecuted for their faith.
level.arians_1658.intro: 1658. Poland has barely survived the Swedish “Deluge”. People look for someone to blame and find them: the Polish Brethren, or Arians, Protestants who rejected the Trinity. Their academy at Raków was closed twenty years ago, and now the Sejm decides their fate. Among them is the philosopher Andrzej Wiszowaty, grandson of the movement's founder Faustus Socinus.
level.arians_1658.fact: The Sejm of 1658 ordered the Arians to convert to Catholicism within three years or leave the country; later the deadline was cut to two. Around 1660 several thousand people left for Transylvania, Prussia and the Netherlands. Wiszowaty settled in Amsterdam and in 1665–1668 published the Bibliotheca Fratrum Polonorum, a multi-volume collection of the Polish Brethren's writings. Their ideas on freedom of conscience and reason in faith were read by John Locke, Pierre Bayle, Voltaire and Newton. And so the country that in 1573 had sworn never to shed blood over faith expelled an entire confession for the first time.
level.arians_1658.source: Constitution of the Sejm of 1658 “On the Arians”; Bibliotheca Fratrum Polonorum (Amsterdam, 1665–1668)
level.ken_1773.title: The First Ministry of Education
level.ken_1773.goal: During the First Partition, Poland creates the Commission of National Education, the first ministry of education in Europe
level.ken_1773.hint: There is money for schools, as long as it isn't pilfered on the way. Whoever is loudest about “distributing” it is the most dangerous of all.
level.ken_1773.intro: 1773. Poland has just lost a third of its lands in the First Partition; the Sejm sits under the eye of the Russian ambassador, and the Sejm's marshal, Adam Poniński, is a paid agent of the neighbours. Then news arrives from Rome: the pope has dissolved the Jesuit order, which ran almost every school in the country.
level.ken_1773.fact: On 14 October 1773 the Sejm established the Commission of National Education, the first state education authority in Europe. It was given the Jesuits' property, and former Jesuits often stayed on as teachers. The Commission published new textbooks in Polish, introduced physics, natural science and even hygiene, and in 1777–1780 Hugo Kołłątaj reformed the Kraków Academy. To be honest, Poniński's Distribution Commission did embezzle a good part of the Jesuit riches, but what remained was enough for the schools to outlive the Partitions themselves.
level.ken_1773.source: Constitution of the Sejm of 14 October 1773; T. Mizia, On the Commission of National Education
level.mickiewicz_1834.title: Pan Tadeusz
level.mickiewicz_1834.goal: After the uprising is crushed, Mickiewicz writes Pan Tadeusz in Paris, a book that became a home for Poles
level.mickiewicz_1834.hint: To believe in forgiveness is to risk everything. The poem is written in exile, and its listeners are those who left with the poet.
level.mickiewicz_1834.intro: 1832. The November Uprising has been crushed. Some ten thousand insurgents, officers, poets and musicians leave through Germany for France; it will be called the Great Emigration. The emperor promises an amnesty to those who return. Among those who left is Adam Mickiewicz, already the most famous poet in Poland.
level.mickiewicz_1834.fact: Many who trusted the amnesty were arrested and exiled. Mickiewicz stayed in Paris and in 1834 published Pan Tadeusz, an epic of a noble manor in Lithuania in 1811–1812, of quarrels, hunts, love and hope in Napoleon. The poem opens with the line “Lithuania, my country, thou art like health”, which Poles know by heart. Paris in those years also held Chopin, Słowacki and Lelewel: the country was gone from the map, but its culture lived on in exile. In 2012 the whole country read Pan Tadeusz aloud in the first National Reading.
level.lodz_1880.title: The Promised Land
level.lodz_1880.goal: A village grows into Łódź, the “Polish Manchester”, where factory owners build palaces and weavers stand at the looms for twelve hours
level.lodz_1880.hint: Cloth needs a buyer, and the biggest buyer lies beyond the eastern customs line. There won't be enough hands if the workers walk out.
level.lodz_1880.intro: The second half of the 19th century. Poland is gone from the map, but chimneys smoke in the Kingdom of Poland. Not long ago Łódź was a village; now Poles, Jews and Germans are flocking here to build factories and work in them. Izrael Poznański started with a shop and is now building a textile empire.
level.lodz_1880.fact: In 1851 the customs border between the Kingdom of Poland and Russia was abolished, and the empire's huge market opened to Polish cloth. After the abolition of serfdom in 1864, peasants poured into Łódź. The city grew faster than any other in Europe: from a few hundred inhabitants in 1820 to about 300,000 by 1900. Poznański built factories, workers' housing and a palace nicknamed “the Louvre of Łódź”. In 1892 the workers of Łódź staged one of the first mass strikes in the empire. Władysław Reymont described the city in his novel The Promised Land, and in 1924 he won the Nobel Prize.
level.flying_university_1885.title: The Flying University
level.flying_university_1885.goal: Women in Warsaw are forbidden to study, so a secret university wanders from flat to flat, and young Maria Skłodowska studies there
level.flying_university_1885.hint: The secret is kept not by a lock but by movement: the courses won't last in one place. Maria will get to Paris in time; first, here.
level.flying_university_1885.intro: 1885. Warsaw, in the Russian Empire. The university teaches only in Russian and does not admit women at all. A teacher, Jadwiga Dawidowa, decides: if it can't be done openly, we will teach in secret.
level.flying_university_1885.fact: From 1885 Dawidowa organised underground courses that became known as the Flying University: classes were held in private flats, in a new place each time, to evade the police. The best Warsaw professors taught history, chemistry, physics and philosophy, in Polish. Thousands of women passed through the courses, among them Maria Skłodowska, who left for Paris in 1891 and later became the first woman to win a Nobel Prize, and twice at that. In 1906 the university came out of hiding as the Society of Scientific Courses.
scene.ask_crown_pl: Ask the Emperor for a Crown
scene.jewels_to_war_pl.action: give the treasury to the army
scene.secret_courses_pl.action: gather a class in a flat
level.przemysl_1295.title: King for Seven Months
level.przemysl_1295.goal: Przemysł II unites Greater Poland with Pomerania and is crowned, and seven months later he is murdered
level.przemysl_1295.hint: A crown goes to whoever holds the lands: the inheritance comes first. It is a king they want dead: a prince without a crown would simply be held for ransom.
level.przemysl_1295.intro: 1294. For a century and a half Poland has been split among rival princes. Przemysł II, Duke of Greater Poland, dreams of more, and luck is on his side: Mściwój, the childless Duke of Gdańsk Pomerania, promises him his lands by the sea. The neighbouring Margraves of Brandenburg watch with hatred.
level.przemysl_1295.fact: Mściwój II died in December 1294, and Przemysł inherited Gdańsk Pomerania. On 26 June 1295 in Gniezno, Archbishop Jakub Świnka crowned him: the first royal coronation in Poland since 1076. Przemysł put a crowned white eagle on his seal, and it has been Poland's coat of arms ever since. He was king for seven months: on 8 February 1296, in the last days of carnival, he was attacked and killed at Rogoźno. Most chroniclers agreed the assassins had been hired by the Margraves of Brandenburg.
level.przemysl_1295.source: Greater Poland Chronicle; Jan Długosz, Annals, under 1295–1296
level.gdansk_1308.title: The Gdańsk Massacre
level.gdansk_1308.goal: Łokietek calls in the Teutonic Knights to save Gdańsk from Brandenburg, and loses Pomerania for a century and a half
level.gdansk_1308.hint: Help was called when there was nothing left to defend with. The Order does not come to the prince: it comes to a city already in trouble.
level.gdansk_1308.intro: 1308. Władysław Łokietek has barely pieced Poland together and is not yet king. The Margraves of Brandenburg march on Gdańsk, the town opens its gates to them, and only the castle holds out. Łokietek has no troops of his own, and his governor takes a fatal step: he asks the neighbours for help, the knights of the Teutonic Order.
level.gdansk_1308.fact: The Knights came, drove out the Brandenburgers, and then on the night of 13 to 14 November 1308 entered the town and carried out a massacre. The death toll is disputed, but the pope later heard a complaint about “ten thousand slain”. Łokietek was handed a bill for the help that he could not pay, and the Order kept Gdańsk and all of Pomerania. Poland only regained them in the Peace of Toruń in 1466, 158 years later. Hence Płowce, and hence Grunwald.
level.gdansk_1308.source: Trials of the King of Poland against the Teutonic Order, 1320–1321 and 1339; Jan Długosz, Annals, under 1308
level.koszyce_1374.title: The Privilege of Koszyce
level.koszyce_1374.goal: The king has only daughters, so he buys them the Polish throne by freeing the nobility from taxes
level.koszyce_1374.hint: Make demands of the nobles and you lose them. A crown for a daughter cannot be won by force: it has to be bought.
level.koszyce_1374.intro: 1374. Casimir the Great, the last Piast on the throne, is dead, and Poland is ruled by his nephew, King Louis of Hungary. He has no sons, only daughters, and Polish custom knows no queens regnant. For the throne to pass to one of them, the nobility must agree.
level.koszyce_1374.fact: On 17 September 1374 in Koszyce, Louis issued a privilege: the nobility was freed from all taxes except two groszy per łan of land, and the king promised not to appoint foreigners to office. In return the nobles recognised his daughter's right to the throne. It was the first general privilege for the nobility, and it set the pattern for centuries: every king after him bought power with new liberties. The daughter turned out to be Jadwiga: in 1384 she was crowned not queen but “king” of Poland.
level.stwosz_1489.title: The Altar of Veit Stoss
level.stwosz_1489.goal: A woodcarver from Nuremberg spends twelve years in Kraków carving the greatest Gothic altarpiece in Europe
level.stwosz_1489.hint: A masterpiece begins with a patron and with patience. Money and signatures are dangerous ground for a craftsman.
level.stwosz_1489.intro: 1477. Kraków is rich: the roads from the Baltic to Hungary and from Germany to Rus run through it. The burghers want their St Mary's Church on the Market Square to outshine all others. They summon the woodcarver Veit Stoss from Nuremberg; in Poland he will be known as Wit Stwosz.
level.stwosz_1489.fact: The altarpiece was consecrated in 1489. It stands about 13 metres high, the apostles are up to 2.7 metres tall and carved from whole linden trunks, and there are some two hundred figures in all. It is said Stoss modelled the saints' faces on Kraków burghers. Back in Nuremberg as a rich man, in 1503 he forged a signature on a bill of exchange and was branded with a red-hot iron on both cheeks. In the Second World War the Nazis carried the altar off to Nuremberg, but after the war it was found and returned to Kraków. Every day its wings are ceremonially opened.
level.stwosz_1489.source: Contract between the Kraków burghers and Veit Stoss (1477); records of the Nuremberg court (1503)
level.wawel_1520.title: The Golden Dome of Wawel
level.wawel_1520.goal: Sigismund the Old and Bona Sforza turn Gothic Wawel into a Renaissance palace, with a chapel and the Sigismund Bell
level.wawel_1520.hint: The master has to reach the court first. Quarrels with envious rivals build no chapels.
level.wawel_1520.intro: 1518. King Sigismund the Old marries the Milanese princess Bona Sforza. With her come Italian tastes to Kraków: vegetables, music, and craftsmen. The Florentine architect Bartolomeo Berrecci is already rebuilding Wawel.
level.wawel_1520.fact: Berrecci built the Sigismund Chapel in 1519–1533; its gilded dome is called the finest Renaissance monument north of the Alps. He also turned Wawel into an Italian palace with arcades. In 1520 the Sigismund Bell was cast for the king, nearly 13 tonnes; it rings only on the most important days, and they say that if you touch its clapper with your left hand, you will find love. Bona also brought “Italian” vegetables to Poland: lettuce, cabbage, leeks, and to this day Poles call a bundle of soup vegetables “włoszczyzna”, “Italian stuff”. Berrecci died in 1537, stabbed in a brawl in Kraków.
level.wawel_1520.source: Inscription in the dome of the Sigismund Chapel; Justus Ludwik Decius, On the Times of King Sigismund
level.warsaw_capital_1596.title: The Capital Moves to Warsaw
level.warsaw_capital_1596.goal: After a fire at Wawel, Sigismund III moves his court to Warsaw, and the town becomes the capital
level.warsaw_capital_1596.hint: A pretext is needed, and one flares up in the royal chambers. If the king decides to rebuild Kraków, he will never go to Warsaw.
level.warsaw_capital_1596.intro: 1595. Sigismund III Vasa is King of Poland and heir to the Swedish throne. Kraków lies on the southern edge of the vast Commonwealth, far from Lithuania and from the sea. The king is fascinated by alchemy, and his chambers at Wawel are full of furnaces and flasks.
level.warsaw_capital_1596.fact: In 1595 fire broke out at Wawel and the north-east wing burned down; rumour stubbornly blamed the king's alchemical experiments. Sigismund rebuilt his chambers but lived more and more in Warsaw, where the Sejm met, and between about 1596 and 1611 the court moved there for good. No official decree moving the capital was ever issued, and kings were still crowned in Kraków. In 1644 his son Władysław IV raised a column to his father in Warsaw, one of the oldest secular monuments in Europe. “Sigismund” with his sabre and cross still stands in Castle Square.
level.khmelnytsky_1648.title: The Khmelnytsky Uprising
level.khmelnytsky_1648.goal: A Cossack captain's personal grievance grows into a war that will shake the Commonwealth to its foundations
level.khmelnytsky_1648.hint: An uprising starts with a wrong, not with a lawsuit. Against the hussars the Cossacks need cavalry, and they can only get it from a neighbour.
level.khmelnytsky_1648.intro: 1647. Along the Dnieper, magnates and their men are taking land from the Cossacks, and the Cossack register has been cut. Bohdan Khmelnytsky, a captain of the Chyhyryn regiment, is a nobleman, educated and respected. The deputy starost Daniel Czapliński has his eye on Khmelnytsky's estate at Subotiv.
level.khmelnytsky_1648.fact: Czapliński seized Subotiv, and Khmelnytsky's son was cruelly flogged. Complaints to the courts and to King Władysław IV came to nothing; legend says the king replied that the Cossacks had sabres. Khmelnytsky fled to the Zaporozhian Sich, was elected hetman, and allied with the Crimean Khan Islam III Giray. In May 1648 at Zhovti Vody and Korsun the Crown army was routed, and the hetmans Mikołaj Potocki and Marcin Kalinowski were taken captive by the Tatars. The war dragged on for years and became one of the bloodiest in the history of these lands: nobles, Cossacks, peasants and hundreds of Jewish communities perished. In Poland it is remembered as the start of the Commonwealth's decline; in Ukraine, as the birth of the Cossack state.
level.khmelnytsky_1648.source: Samuel Twardowski, The Civil War; Cossack chronicles of the Eyewitness and of Hrabianka
level.august2_1697.title: Augustus the Strong
level.august2_1697.goal: The Elector of Saxony changes his faith, outruns the elected Frenchman, and takes the Polish throne
level.august2_1697.hint: A Catholic throne needs a Catholic: that comes first. Whoever arrives first with an army is king; the rival will get the message.
level.august2_1697.intro: 1697. Jan Sobieski is dead. The richest candidate is the French Prince of Conti, backed by the primate and most of the votes. But the Elector of Saxony, Frederick Augustus, has money, an army next door, and hands of iron: they say he bends horseshoes with his fingers. There is just one problem: he is a Lutheran.
level.august2_1697.fact: On 1 June 1697 the Elector secretly converted to Catholicism. On 27 June the primate proclaimed Conti king, but part of the nobility proclaimed Augustus, and the Saxon marched into Poland with his army first. On 15 September he was crowned in Wawel Cathedral, though not by the primate but by the Bishop of Kuyavia. Conti only reached the Bay of Gdańsk with a French squadron in September, saw that it was all settled, and sailed home. So began the “Saxon era”: Augustus dragged the country into the Great Northern War, and in 1717 the Silent Sejm, watched over by Russian troops, cut the Commonwealth's army to 24,000, with almost no one allowed to speak.
level.august2_1697.source: Diaries of the 1697 election; Kazimierz Jarochowski, History of the Reign of Augustus II
level.bar_1768.title: The Bar Confederation
level.bar_1768.goal: The ambassador arrests bishops, the nobility rises at Bar, and young Pułaski holds Jasna Góra
level.bar_1768.hint: A rising needs a pretext, and the ambassador will supply it. Not every daring act is heroic: lay hands on the king and all Europe will curse you.
level.bar_1768.intro: 1767. In Warsaw, the Russian ambassador Nikolai Repnin gives all the orders. Under his pressure the Sejm is to confirm the rights of religious dissenters and the empress's guarantees. Opposing him are Kajetan Sołtyk, Bishop of Kraków, and a few other senators.
level.bar_1768.fact: On the night of 13 to 14 October 1767 Repnin had Sołtyk, another bishop and two senators arrested and taken to Kaluga, where they spent five years. On 29 February 1768 at Bar in Podolia the nobility formed a confederation “for faith and freedom”. The war lasted four years; Kazimierz Pułaski won fame defending Jasna Góra in 1770–1771. But in 1771 the confederates kidnapped King Stanisław August, who escaped that same night, and Pułaski was branded a regicide. He left for America, became the “father of the American cavalry”, and fell at Savannah in 1779. The confederation was crushed, and in 1772 came the First Partition.
level.bar_1768.source: Act of the Bar Confederation (1768); Władysław Konopczyński, The Bar Confederation
level.targowica_1792.title: Targowica
level.targowica_1792.goal: Magnates invite a foreign army against the Constitution of 3 May; Prince Józef wins at Zieleńce, but the king gives in
level.targowica_1792.hint: The enemy will not come without its ally. Victory in the field is not yet victory: the king will decide.
level.targowica_1792.intro: 1792. A year ago Poland adopted the Constitution of 3 May. The magnates who lost power, Szczęsny Potocki, Ksawery Branicki and Seweryn Rzewuski, travel to St Petersburg to see Empress Catherine II.
level.targowica_1792.fact: The act of confederation was signed in St Petersburg on 27 April 1792 and proclaimed in the small town of Targowica; in May a Russian army of a hundred thousand crossed the border. On 18 June at Zieleńce Prince Józef Poniatowski defeated a Russian corps, and to honour the victory the king founded the Virtuti Militari, Poland's highest military decoration to this day; Poniatowski and Kościuszko were the first to receive it. But on 24 July the king joined Targowica, the army laid down its arms, and Poniatowski and Kościuszko resigned. A year later came the Second Partition. In Polish, “targowiczanin”, a man of Targowica, still means a traitor.
level.targowica_1792.source: Act of the Targowica Confederation (1792); Emanuel Rostworowski, The Last King of the Commonwealth
level.grodno_1795.title: The Silent Sejm and the Last King
level.grodno_1795.goal: In Grodno, under the guns, the Sejm “consents” to the Second Partition by silence, and two years later the king abdicates
level.grodno_1795.hint: Protest stops nothing here: it just removes a man from the chamber. Abdication is signed when the state is already gone.
level.grodno_1795.intro: 1793. After Targowica, the last Sejm of the Commonwealth is summoned in Grodno. The Russian ambassador Jakob Sievers has bribed some of the deputies, the rest are surrounded by troops, and cannon are trained on the chamber. The Second Partition must be ratified.
level.grodno_1795.fact: On 23 September 1793, after the deputies had sat silent for hours, the marshal declared that “silence means consent”, and the Second Partition treaty was ratified. Deputies who protested were arrested. A year later the Kościuszko Uprising broke out, and after its defeat, in 1795, Russia, Prussia and Austria divided what was left of the country. On 25 November 1795, Catherine II's name day, Stanisław August signed his abdication in Grodno. He died in St Petersburg in 1798. Poland would vanish from the map for 123 years.
level.grodno_1795.source: Diary of the Grodno Sejm of 1793; Act of Abdication of Stanisław August (1795)
level.raszyn_1809.title: Raszyn: Give Up the Capital to Win the War
level.raszyn_1809.goal: Prince Józef yields Warsaw to the Austrians, and while they sit in it, he takes half of Galicia from Austria
level.raszyn_1809.hint: Cling to the capital and you die in it. Let the enemy sit in Warsaw while the army goes where no one expects it.
level.raszyn_1809.intro: 1809. Napoleon is at war with Austria, and an Austrian army of 30,000 under Archduke Ferdinand marches on the small Duchy of Warsaw. Prince Józef Poniatowski has two or three times fewer soldiers.
level.raszyn_1809.fact: On 19 April 1809 at Raszyn the Poles held off the Austrians all day, then withdrew. Poniatowski made an agreement, surrendered Warsaw without a fight, and led the army to the right bank of the Vistula, and then turned south into Austrian Galicia: he took Lublin, Sandomierz and Zamość, and on 15 July entered Kraków. With their rear gone, the Austrians left Warsaw. Under the Treaty of Schönbrunn the Duchy gained Kraków and West Galicia and grew by almost half.
level.raszyn_1809.source: Treaty of Schönbrunn (1809); Szymon Askenazy, Prince Józef Poniatowski
level.leipzig_1813.title: The Honour of the Poles
level.leipzig_1813.goal: Prince Józef receives a marshal's baton at the Battle of the Nations, and three days later dies in the Elster covering the retreat
level.leipzig_1813.hint: He was offered salvation, by another emperor. The baton goes to the one who stayed loyal.
level.leipzig_1813.intro: 1813. The Grande Armée has perished in Russia, and the Duchy of Warsaw is occupied by the Russians. Through go-betweens, Tsar Alexander offers Prince Józef Poniatowski the chance to change sides. The prince leads what is left of the Polish army to Napoleon in Saxony.
level.leipzig_1813.fact: Poniatowski answered the offers by saying that he had been entrusted with the honour of the Poles. On 16 October 1813, the first day of the Battle of the Nations at Leipzig, Napoleon made him a Marshal of France, the only foreigner among his marshals. On 19 October the prince and his Poles covered the retreat; the bridge over the Elster was blown too early, and the wounded Poniatowski rode his horse into the river and drowned. His last words are said to have been: “God has entrusted me with the honour of the Poles; to God alone will I return it.” He rests at Wawel beside the kings.
level.leipzig_1813.source: Bulletins of the Grande Armée (1813); Szymon Askenazy, Prince Józef Poniatowski
level.kingdom_1815.title: The Kingdom of Poland
level.kingdom_1815.goal: The Congress of Vienna creates a Kingdom of Poland with the tsar as king and a liberal constitution, and the tsar's brother at the head of the army
level.kingdom_1815.hint: A constitution is given to a kingdom, and the kingdom must be bargained for first. The tsar never did make his friend viceroy.
level.kingdom_1815.intro: 1815. Napoleon is beaten. In Vienna the monarchs are redrawing Europe, and the fate of the Polish lands is one of the thorniest questions. At Tsar Alexander I's side stands Prince Adam Jerzy Czartoryski, his friend from youth and a former Russian foreign minister.
level.kingdom_1815.fact: The Congress of Vienna created the Kingdom of Poland in union with Russia: the tsar became King of Poland. On 27 November 1815 Alexander I granted it a constitution, one of the most liberal in Europe at the time: its own Sejm, army and courts, and Polish as the language of government. Czartoryski hoped to be viceroy, but the post went to the old general Józef Zajączek, and Grand Duke Constantine took command of the army. Bit by bit the constitution was ignored, and fifteen years later came the November Night.
level.kingdom_1815.source: Final Act of the Congress of Vienna (1815); Constitutional Charter of the Kingdom of Poland
level.krakow_1846.title: 1846: Uprising and Massacre
level.krakow_1846.goal: The nobility rises for freedom, but the peasants of Galicia, remembering serf labour, turn not with them but against them
level.krakow_1846.hint: The promise came too late: the one who believes is not the one being promised, but the one who remembers the corvée. The rising will end with a procession.
level.krakow_1846.intro: February 1846. A rising across all of Poland is being prepared, centred on the Free City of Kraków, a tiny republic watched over by three powers. In Austrian Galicia peasants still owe serf labour, and to them the lords are not brothers in the nation but masters.
level.krakow_1846.fact: On 22 February a National Government was proclaimed in Kraków, abolishing serf labour and granting land to the peasants. But in Galicia peasants led by Jakub Szela, egged on by Austrian officials who paid for every “rebel”, sacked hundreds of manor houses and killed about a thousand people: nobles, stewards, priests. On 27 February the revolutionary philosopher Edward Dembowski went out to meet the peasants near Podgórze with a religious procession and was shot by Austrian soldiers. The rising collapsed and Kraków was annexed by Austria. Szela was given land in Bukovina by the authorities, and in 1848 serf labour in Galicia was abolished after all, by the Austrians themselves.
level.krakow_1846.source: Stefan Kieniewicz, The Peasant Movement in Galicia in 1846
level.poznan_1848.title: Springtime of Nations in Poznań
level.poznan_1848.goal: The revolution in Berlin frees Poles from prison, and in Greater Poland a rising of scythemen begins
level.poznan_1848.hint: First the prisoner has to walk free. Disband your units for the sake of promises and there will be no one left to fight.
level.poznan_1848.intro: March 1848. The Springtime of Nations sweeps across Europe. In Berlin's Moabit prison sits Ludwik Mierosławski, sentenced to death for preparing the rising of 1846. In Poznań the Poles form a National Committee and wait for the King of Prussia to grant them self-rule.
level.poznan_1848.fact: On 20 March 1848 a Berlin crowd freed the Polish prisoners, and Mierosławski and his comrades were driven through Berlin in an open carriage to cries of “Long live Poland!”. Units gathered in Greater Poland, joined by peasant scythemen. On 11 April, under the Jarosławiec agreement, most units were disbanded in exchange for a promised “national reorganisation”, but the Prussians broke their word. On 30 April the insurgents won at Miłosław, and by 9 May they had surrendered. After that, Greater Poland fought not with weapons but with “organic work”: schools, banks, cooperatives.
level.poznan_1848.source: Ludwik Mierosławski, The Poznań Rising of 1848
level.school_strike_1905.title: The School Strike
level.school_strike_1905.goal: During the 1905 revolution, Warsaw schoolboys walk out of Russian schools, and win Polish ones
level.school_strike_1905.hint: Giving in means losing here. First comes the grown-ups' example, then courage, then a new school.
level.school_strike_1905.intro: 1905. The Kingdom of Poland. In the gymnasiums everything is taught in Russian, even Polish; a Polish word spoken in the break can be punished. In January troops fire on workers in St Petersburg, and strikes break out across the empire.
level.school_strike_1905.fact: In January and February 1905 gymnasium pupils in Warsaw and other towns declared a boycott of the state school, demanding teaching in Polish and Polish teachers. The boycott held for years, and thousands of pupils left the state schools. The authorities gave way and allowed private schools teaching in Polish, and in 1905 the Polish School Society was founded, opening hundreds of schools and reading rooms. Ten years later many of the striking schoolboys joined the Legions.
level.school_strike_1905.source: Statute of the Polish School Society (1905)
level.kadrowka_1914.title: The First Cadre Company
level.kadrowka_1914.goal: In the first days of the Great War, Piłsudski's riflemen tear down the partition border posts and march on Kielce
level.kadrowka_1914.hint: First the company has to be formed. A town does not have to be taken by storm: you can just march in.
level.kadrowka_1914.intro: August 1914. For the first time, the three partitioning powers are at war with one another: Austria-Hungary and Germany against Russia. Poles serve in all three armies. In Austrian Kraków, Józef Piłsudski has spent years building rifle associations, and he is waiting for this hour.
level.kadrowka_1914.fact: On 6 August 1914 the First Cadre Company, some 150 riflemen, marched out of the Oleandry in Kraków. At Michałowice they tore down the border posts between Austria and Russia and headed north. On 12 August the company entered Kielce, but the town greeted it coldly: people feared Russian revenge and did not believe it would succeed. These riflemen grew into the Polish Legions, and the song “We Are the First Brigade” became one of Poland's great soldiers' songs.
level.kadrowka_1914.source: Piłsudski's order of 6 August 1914; Wacław Lipiński, The Struggle for Independence
level.act_1916.title: The Act of 5 November
level.act_1916.goal: Germany and Austria proclaim a Kingdom of Poland to raise soldiers, and Piłsudski demands a government first
level.act_1916.hint: A promise without power will bring no soldiers, but only failure will make the Germans give way. It is too early to leave.
level.act_1916.intro: 1916. German and Austrian troops have taken the Russian part of Poland. Hundreds of thousands are dying at Verdun and on the Somme, and Berlin needs new soldiers. The Governor-General of Warsaw, Hans von Beseler, has a proposal: promise the Poles a state, and they will join the army.
level.act_1916.fact: On 5 November 1916 in Warsaw and Lublin, the act of the two emperors creating an “independent Kingdom of Poland” was read out: with no king, no government and no fixed borders. A week later volunteers were called up, but only a handful came: the Poles, as Piłsudski put it, would not give soldiers without a government of their own. In January 1917 the Provisional Council of State was formed, and Piłsudski headed its military commission. For the first time since the partitions, the great powers were talking about a Polish state, and they could no longer take their words back.
level.act_1916.source: Act of 5 November 1916; Andrzej Garlicki, Józef Piłsudski
